    Smooth reduced equations on an open profile domain reconstruct a slice-wise pressure satisfying the physical momentum equation on each selected open convex spatial slice.

    The stream equation supplies the curl, and the two evolution equations supply its transport. The time set may exclude a singular endpoint. The pressure is constructed separately on each time slice.

    The Cartesian velocity has finite kinetic energy when the reduced swirl, streamfunction, and its two physical derivatives have finite r³ dr dz moments. The streamfunction moment fixes the decay normalization; the independent swirl moment is not replaced by a bound on its derivatives.

    The energy formula follows by applying the radial cancellation on almost every axial slice, then the cylindrical change of variables. No trace at infinity or integrability of the velocity is an input.

    Reduced viscous equations on an open profile domain D give the Cartesian vorticity equation at every spacetime point whose (t, s, z) image lies in D. Axis points are covered exactly when D contains a neighbourhood of s = 0, so the profiles must be smooth for slightly negative squared radius as well; this is the even-in-r condition of classical axisymmetric flow. The stream equation identifying this vorticity with curl is a separate condition. Setting viscosity to zero gives the Euler transport equation.

  (ν a b c d e f : ℝ) (ha : a ≠ 0) (hheat : e = ν * c)

    structure CAS.Continuum.GaussianRule (a b : ℝ) (w : ℝ → ℝ)
  (hw : ContinuousOn w (Set.uIcc a b)) (n : ℕ) : Type
    structure CAS.Continuum.GaussianRule (a b : ℝ)
  (w : ℝ → ℝ)
  (hw : ContinuousOn w (Set.uIcc a b))
  (n : ℕ) : Type

    A Gaussian rule on [a, b] for the weight w: n distinct nodes in (a, b), positive weights, and exactness against w for every polynomial of degree below 2n.

    Fields

    nodes : Fin n → ℝ

    The points where the rule evaluates its integrand.

    weights : Fin n → ℝ

    The coefficient multiplying the integrand at each node.

    injective : Function.Injective self.nodes

    The nodes are pairwise distinct, so the Lagrange basis and the Hermite interpolant on them exist.

    interior : ∀ (i : Fin n), self.nodes i ∈ Set.Ioo a b

    Every node lies in the open interval (a, b), where the integrand is sampled.

    positive : ∀ (i : Fin n), 0 < self.weights i

    Every weight is strictly positive, which makes the rule stable under uniform perturbation of the integrand.

    exact : ∀ (p : Polynomial ℝ),
  p.natDegree < 2 * n →
    ∑ i, self.weights i * Polynomial.eval (self.nodes i) p = (CAS.Continuum.polynomialIntegral a b w hw) p

    The rule integrates every polynomial of degree below 2n exactly against w: ∑ i, weights i * p (nodes i) = ∫_a^b p w.

    structure CAS.Continuum.RationalInterval.Precision :

    Numerical precision policy for automatic interval compilation.

    The defaults use exponential Taylor order 8, square roots with 12 binary digits, 10 logarithm series terms, and subdivision depth 2.

    Fields

    expOrder : ℕ

    Taylor order for exponential and hyperbolic ranges; zero is promoted to one.

    sqrtDigits : ℕ

    Binary digits of square-root enclosures.

    logTerms : ℕ

    Series terms for logarithm ranges, run by FloatLib at degree 2 * max logTerms 1.

    depth : ℕ

    Number of checked bisection levels used by subdivided enclosures.

    digits : Option ℕ

    class CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.{u} (ι : Type u) : Type u
    class CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.{u}
  (ι : Type u) : Type u

    A CEGA-facing real interval backend.

    The backend chooses the interval representation. CEGA only asks for lower and upper real endpoints plus sound projections from backend membership to real inequalities, so any representation with these projections fits the same API; RationalInterval is the one instance.

    The interface permits empty enclosures: it does not require lo I ≤ hi I. Any inhabited enclosure has ordered endpoints by lower_mem and upper_mem.

    Methods

    Lower real endpoint.

    hi : ι → ℝ

    MemReal : ι → ℝ → Prop

    Backend membership predicate, interpreted over real values.

    lower_mem : ∀ {I : ι} {x : ℝ}, CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.MemReal I x → CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.lo I ≤ x

    Membership implies the lower endpoint bound.

    upper_mem : ∀ {I : ι} {x : ℝ}, CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.MemReal I x → x ≤ CAS.Continuum.RealIntervalBackend.hi I

    def CAS.Tactic.Certificate.closeFromLocalCertificates :
  Lean.Elab.Tactic.TacticM Unit
    def CAS.Tactic.Certificate.closeFromLocalCertificates :
  Lean.Elab.Tactic.TacticM Unit

    Close the main goal from a matching checked certificate in the local context or among the subterms of the target.

    Exact projections are tried first. Approximation, residual, bound, model, and quadrature certificates may then be weakened to a larger requested budget; enclosures may be widened at both endpoints. Every generated inequality must be discharged by the shared arithmetic phase. A certificate whose domain differs from the goal's is then restricted to the goal's domain (inferSubsetProof) and tried again in the same way.

    lineDerivCLM 𝕜 v is the continuous 𝕜-linear-map sending a distribution T : 𝓓'^{k}_{K}(E, F) to its derivative along the vector v, which is a distribution in 𝓓^{n}_{K}(E, F). Because differentiating increases the order, this only makes sense if k + 1 ≤ n, otherwise we define it as the zero map.

    The parameters n and k are implicit as they can often be inferred from context, or specified by a type ascription. For n = k = ⊤, we also provide instances of the LineDeriv notation typeclass.

    Unlike the residual-and-assigned-value PDEProblem interface, this structure records enough regularity for every derivative in the equation to have its analytic meaning. It also distinguishes the assigned value at t = 0 from the limit u(x, t) → g(x₀) as (x, t) → (x₀, 0) with t > 0.

    differentiableAt_time : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → DifferentiableAt ℝ (u x) t

    differentiableAt_space : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun y ↦ u y t) x

    At every positive time, the spatial slice of the solution is differentiable.

    residual_eq : ∀ (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → HeatEquation.heatParabolicOperator u x t = f x t

    The pointwise forced heat-equation residual vanishes at positive time.

    initial_value : ∀ (x : ℝ^n), u x 0 = g x

    The explicitly assigned value at time zero is the initial datum.

    Kaplan's lifespan bound. Let w ≥ 0 be a Dirichlet eigenfunction of -Δ on Ω with eigenvalue λ > 0, normalized by ∫ w = 1, and let g ≥ 0 have η₀ = ∫ w g > λ. A solution of uₜ - Δu = u² on [0, T] that is C² in the open cylinder, continuous on its closure, zero on the lateral boundary and equal to g at time zero has T ≤ λ⁻¹ log (η₀ / (η₀ - λ)). This is the time at which the solution of η' = η² - λ η from η₀ blows up.

    On a nonempty bounded connected open domain, domain geometry supplies a normalized positive first eigenfunction for which sufficiently large initial moments exclude a nonnegative weak solution up to the prescribed time.

    The forcing must represent the nonlinear reaction against every H¹₀ test. The explicit sufficient threshold is written using the decreasing power m₀^(1-p). No moment differential inequality is part of the hypotheses.

    The heat-kernel evolution preserves uniform bounds.

    If the continuous initial datum satisfies |g| ≤ M, then its heat evolution satisfies the same pointwise bound at every time; taking the optimal M, this is the L∞ contraction property of the heat semigroup. For t ≤ 0 this is the bound on g itself. For t > 0, positivity of the Gaussian kernel, its unit mass, and the Bochner integral triangle inequality give

    An order-m time jet whose successive derivatives take values in

    H^m(Omega), H^{m-1}(Omega), ..., H^0(Omega).

    Each time derivative spends one spatial derivative in this regularity budget; see Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 6 for its use in the wave equation. The recursive core requires adjacent entries to be weak time derivatives, so the entries describe one trajectory and its derivatives.

    Choose one coherent finite family of dual-valued Dirichlet forcing representatives from an order-m Sobolev time jet.

    At reverse index r, the chosen function represents the Dirichlet load of the corresponding iterated jet tail. For every adjacent pair, the higher-index function is absolutely continuous and its strong derivative is the lower-index function almost everywhere.

    Assume the divergence-form weak wave identity holds almost everywhere in time and that both f(t) and u_{tt}(t) are essentially bounded in L²(Omega). On a domain carrying the operational C2BoundaryAtlas, assume uniformly elliptic W¹,∞ principal coefficients with global C¹ representatives.     Evans Section 7.2.3: differentiated Galerkin limit with bounded nonsymmetric lower-order terms.

    Let the autonomous wave operator split as B = A + R. The principal part A is symmetric and coercive on the energy space, while R is allowed to be nonsymmetric and is controlled in the mixed V x H norm. Stable dense trial projections, compatible ambient initial data, a coherent forcing chain, and the uniform forcing budget generate a finite chain of ambient weak-wave solutions for the full operator A + R, provided hRitz holds:

    (A + R) (q r.succ - P_k (q r.succ)) w = 0

    for every trial level k, adjacent jet index r, and test w in that trial space. Here P_k is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to V. This full-operator condition is separate from stability and density.

    All finite-dimensional trajectories, their uniform bounds, and their common weak limit are constructed in the proof. In particular, no limiting weak wave or higher-regularity conclusion is included among the hypotheses.

    Finite restart of the short-interval Evans uniqueness argument.

    The points τ 0, …, τ N form an ordered finite partition of [a,b]. Each adjacent interval is short enough for estimate (40), and hcover records that these intervals cover the full time domain. Induction carries both zero traces from one partition point to the next; the velocity trace is recovered from the vanishing displacement by weak derivative uniqueness.

    The partition is explicit so this theorem is useful beyond uniform meshes: applications may refine only where coefficient bounds require it.

    Evans, §7.2.2 weak-wave uniqueness with coefficient-level assumptions.

    Unlike eq_of_evans_coefficients, this theorem has no scalar IntervalIntegrable hypotheses. The L² solution types and homogeneous weak equation provide integrability of B(u,v), hence of A(u,v)=B(u,v)-R(u,v). Strong measurability is needed only for Adot and R, the two fields not already represented by the weak equation. In concrete divergence form it follows from measurability of the coefficient fields. hAdotBound follows from uniform bounds on the time derivative of the principal coefficients. hRBound puts the H norm on the solution slot, so it follows from uniform bounds on c, b and div b after a spatial integration by parts; bounds on b alone do not give it.

    The projected Galerkin spatial equations are closed under Evans's weak compactness limit.

    At level n, the acceleration is only the residual precomposed with the trial projection:

    accelerationₙ = (ell - B(·)uₙ) ∘ Pₙ.

    This is the finite-dimensional statement: in general a Galerkin approximation does not solve the ambient equation in all of V*. Uniform energy stability and Pₙv → v imply strong convergence of the lifted projections on L²(V). Pairing the weakly convergent residuals against those strongly convergent tests identifies the acceleration limit with ell - B(·)u, and hence recovers the full ambient equation only at the limit.

    Evans's backward estimate for a fixed canonical displacement evolution.

    The preceding theorem constructs an evolution together with the estimate. Canonical-representative uniqueness shows that the endpoint norm is independent of that construction, so the same inequality holds for any ContinuousPivotEvolutionOn representing the displacement. This nonexistential form is the one used by the Grönwall and interval-restart arguments.

    Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(i): abstract Galerkin form.

    Assume a bounded projected Galerkin family with the same exact initial displacement q₀ and velocity p₀ at every index. Suppose in addition that estimate (52) has supplied dimension-independent essential bounds

    ‖uₘ(t)‖_V ≤ Cᵤ and ‖uₘ'(t)‖_H ≤ Cᵥ.

    Then the compactness construction produces a weak solution satisfying

    u ∈ L∞(a,b;V) and u_t ∈ L∞(a,b;H),

    with the same almost-everywhere bounds. In concrete divergence-form wave problems, ae_norm_displacementLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le and ae_norm_velocityLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le supply these two additional hypotheses from the coercive Galerkin energy estimate.

    The proof uses the same common ultrafilter for displacement, velocity, and acceleration. The weak-wave equations are passed to the limit exactly as in exists_of_bounded_projected_galerkin_family, while improvedRegularity_of_weak_L2_limits preserves the closed convex essential norm balls. Thus the regularity conclusion is proved rather than stored as extra data in the definition of a weak solution.

    Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(ii): identification of the differentiated Galerkin limits.

    Suppose one common filter gives weak limits for an original Galerkin family and its differentiated family. The exact finite-dimensional identities

    J (duₘ) = velocityₘ,

    J* (dvelocityₘ) = accelerationₘ

    then survive weak convergence. If the coefficient derivative identity d uₘ/dt = duₘ is also retained in the identity Gelfand triple, the limit du is the V-valued weak derivative of u.

    Uniform essential bounds on duₘ in V and dvelocityₘ in H pass to the same limits by weak closedness of the almost-everywhere norm balls. Finally, for an autonomous operator and weakly differentiable forcing, the theorem constructs u_{ttt} in L²(a,b;V*).

    This is the compactness/identification step that cannot be justified by extracting unrelated subnets for the original and differentiated systems.

    Weak sequential/net closure of Evans's weak-wave solution predicate.

    Suppose a family of weak-wave solutions has a common weak limit in the three natural Bochner spaces:

    • displacement in L²(a,b;V),
    • velocity in L²(a,b;H), and
    • acceleration in L²(a,b;V*).

    The acceleration convergence is stated after Riesz transport, matching the Hilbert weak topology used by the compactness theorem. Then the three limit objects again satisfy the weak-wave predicate with the same initial data and forcing.

    The proof follows the Evans limit passage:

    1. bounded linearity of H → V* passes the displacement identity;
    2. fixed space-time testing passes the velocity identity; and
    3. bounded operator-valued multiplication passes B(t)u weakly, so uniqueness of weak limits yields u_tt + B(t)u = ell in L²(V*).

    structure NavierStokes.LerayHopfSolution {n : ℕ}
  (nse : NavierStokes.Problem n) : Type

    Pressure-free Leray-Hopf solution on [0,T].

    The weak momentum equation and incompressibility come from WeakSolution. The additional fields give velocity and gradient Bochner bounds, continuity into the weak topology of L², the initial trace as equality of L² classes, force-work integrability, and the all-time energy inequality measured from the prescribed datum.

    The initial datum is required only in L². Spatial-gradient membership and its weak derivative identity are imposed on (0,T], while the velocity and its initial trace are defined on [0,T]. These representative requirements at every positive time are stronger than an almost-everywhere formulation.

    Pressure-retaining weak solution to the Navier-Stokes equations on [0,T].

    This is a distributional solution notion in its own right, not a regularity extension of PointwiseResidualSolution. The velocity carries a distributional spatial-gradient witness. The momentum identity uses test fields that may be nonzero at the initial time and therefore contains the prescribed initial datum as a boundary term. This avoids identifying initial data through an arbitrary value assigned to a representative at the measure-zero slice t = 0.

    This is a pressure-retaining, strong-data interface: pressure and forcing have L² spatial slices at every time, while weak_momentum_integrable_on separately gives integrability of the summed iterated integrand.

    Pressure is retained, so the test field is a general compactly supported vector field. The separate distributionallyDivergenceFree_at field records distributional incompressibility.     The integrability obligations behind the iterated weak momentum integral.

    Lean's Bochner integral is totalized, so an identity between bare integral expressions would not by itself assert that the displayed pairings are analytic integrals. This predicate records spatial integrability at every physical time and outer time integrability. The initial boundary pairing is integrable automatically from the stored L² initial datum and compact support of the test field.

    Pressure-free weak Navier-Stokes solution on the closed slab [0,T].

    The momentum equation is imposed only against smooth compactly supported solenoidal tests, so pressure does not occur. The raw fields retain representatives because the weak-derivative and nonlinear-pairing definitions are representative based.     Evans, §3.2.4: local existence from a regular characteristic flow.

    Given compatible boundary gradients, a noncharacteristic basepoint, and the regular characteristic flow of (31), there are open neighborhoods W₀ of the boundary parameter and V of the boundary point together with a C² function u such that

    • F(Du,u,x)=0 on V,
    • u(boundary(y))=data(y) and Du(boundary(y))=initialGradient(y) for y∈W₀, and
    • every point of V lies in the requested ambient domain Ω.

    Both the residual and Du = p are derived from the characteristic and first-variation ODEs. The identity Du = p ∘ coords then gives a C¹ derivative, hence the C² regularity in Evans's Theorem 2. This theorem takes a regular characteristic flow as input; SmoothConstruction constructs that flow from boundary and value data.

    Uniqueness of affine Carathéodory solutions in a Banach space on their prescribed interval.

    The theorem applies to any two inhabitants of AffineCaratheodorySolutionOn. Subtracting the two a.e. equations eliminates the forcing. The vector-valued absolutely continuous FTC turns the result into

    w(t) = ∫ₐᵗ A(s)w(s) ds,

    and the scalar zero-data integral Grönwall lemma applied to ‖w(t)‖ proves that w vanishes. Equality is asserted on [a,b], since the solution structure imposes no conditions outside that interval.

    Quantitative Hilbert-valued one-dimensional H¹ estimate.

    If u, du ∈ L²(a,b;H) and du is the weak time derivative of u, then the Lions–Magenes representative is continuous on [a,b] and satisfies

    ‖u(t)‖ ≤ sqrt (‖u‖² / (b-a) + 2 ‖u‖ ‖du‖)

    at every time in the closed interval. It agrees almost everywhere with the original Bochner trajectory, so the same explicit estimate holds almost everywhere for that trajectory.

    The constant is the standard non-sharp one-dimensional Sobolev estimate: choose an interior time where the squared norm equals its interval average, then apply the exact Hilbert-space energy identity and L² Hölder on the subinterval joining that time to t.

    existsUnique_of_measurable_galerkin_garding_L2 constructs the unique Bochner class solving the integrated weak equation. This theorem adds the data that Evans uses to define the parabolic weak solution and its a priori theory:

    • the weak time derivative belongs to L²(a,b;V*);
    • u_t = ell - B(·)u almost everywhere;
    • the state has a representative continuous from [a,b] into the pivot Hilbert space H, with left trace equal to uInit;
    • the representative satisfies the Gårding energy estimate on every prefix [a,t].

    Thus the measurable Galerkin construction produces a weak solution in the sense of Evans §7.1.1, with the continuity into H that Evans obtains from §5.9.2, Theorem 3.

The improved Galerkin estimate uses only the load's L² norm, so density and coercive completion pass both the solution and its L²(H) time derivative to an arbitrary Bochner load. The functions A, Adot, and R are fixed across these forcing approximations, and A remains time-dependent in the limiting equation. The derivative bound N of the principal form contributes N/2 beside the remainder's coefficient L² in the energy budget. Principal coercivity gives the L∞(V) bound; coercivity of the full form supplies the basic L²(V) estimate and continuous dependence on the load.

    The hypothesis

    theta ‖v‖_V² ≤ B(t)(v,v) + gamma ‖v‖_H²

    is the abstract form of the estimate (22) that Evans uses for parabolic operators with lower-order terms (§7.1.2). For the difference w of two solutions, the Lions–Magenes identity yields

    Let V ↪ H be a compact Gelfand inclusion and let a family of trajectories be uniformly bounded in L²(a,b;V), with dual time derivatives uniformly bounded in L²(a,b;V*). If a < b, then the included trajectories have compact closure in L²(a,b;H).

  (u : ℝ^n → ℝ) : Prop

    u is a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u) on Ω: on every open V with compact closure in Ω, every W^{1,2}(V) element that represents u has no more energy than its perturbation by any smooth function with compact support in V.

    The perturbations may be large, and they are the smallest class in use, so among the notions that compare with all perturbations in a class this is the weakest. Nothing is asked of u outside such sets V, and Ω need not be bounded.

    The predicate does not say that u is in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω): on a set V where u has no representative in W^{1,2}(V) it asks nothing. It does not say that the energies are finite either: the integrals are Bochner integrals, which are 0 for a density that is not integrable. The regularity theorems assume IsLocallyWkpOn 1 2 Ω u and a density with Lipschitz gradient, for which every energy is finite (integrable_gradientDensity_of_lipschitzWith).

    A classical solution of the Euler–Lagrange equation is analytic. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be open and let F be real-analytic on ℝⁿ with θ ‖ξ‖² ≤ D²F(p)(ξ, ξ) ≤ Λ ‖ξ‖² for all p and ξ, where θ > 0. Every function v of class C² on Ω that satisfies div(∇F(∇v)) = 0 at every point of Ω is real-analytic on Ω.

    The function v is a local minimizer by isLocalMinimizerOn_of_contDiffOn_two, and a continuous local minimizer is analytic by analyticOnNhd_of_isLocalMinimizerOn_of_continuousOn.

The energy may be infinite and no global upper growth assumption is imposed on either the density or its gradient derivative.

    A weak solution minimizes a jointly convex mixed density in its affine Sobolev class. Here D(x) is the full derivative at (u(x), ∇u(x)), and the weak equation tests its value and gradient components together.

    Competitors may have infinite energy, and any finite-energy competitor forces the solution's energy to be finite. The domain is arbitrary, the dimension may be zero, and the Sobolev exponent may be 1 or ∞.

M K₀ⁱ near each point by the maximum principle (SolutionOnBall.exists_familyNorm_le), and such bounds give a convergent Taylor series.

    Analyticity of solutions of Euler–Lagrange equations with analytic density. Let Ω ⊆ ℝ^n be open and let u be smooth on Ω with div(∇F(∇u)) = 0 at every point of Ω. If F is real-analytic at the gradients ∇u(x), x ∈ Ω, and its Hessian is positive definite at these gradients, then u is real-analytic on Ω. All dimensions and all open sets; the ellipticity constant may depend on the point, and F need not be convex or analytic away from the gradients of u. The derivative bounds of exists_iteratedCoordinateNorm_le_of_gradientDensity make the Taylor series of u converge.

    structure PDE.Hyperbolic.ConservationLaw.Scalar.IsWeakSolution
  (flux : ℝ → ℝ)
  (U : TopologicalSpace.Opens ℝ^2)
  (u : ℝ^2 → ℝ) : Prop

    Weak solution in the standard test-function formulation.

    The domain is open, both u and flux ∘ u are locally integrable there, and the distributional identity

    ∫ (u φ_t + flux(u) φ_x) = 0

    holds for every compactly supported C¹ test function. The displayed integrand is integrable because both coefficients are locally integrable and the derivatives of the test function are continuous and compactly supported in the domain.

    This is the interior distributional equation on U. It is not the weak half-space initial-value formulation: no initial datum or boundary term at t = 0 is part of this structure.

    Fields

    Local integrability of the conserved quantity.

    Local integrability of the flux.

    A local weak Riemann solution from C² strict hyperbolicity and the genuinely nonlinear or linearly degenerate alternative for every ordered family.

    One radius, state bound and propagation speed work for every sufficiently close right state. The same constructed function is the finite gluing of ordered weak waves whose successive endpoint states satisfy IsElementaryConnection. It satisfies the initial weak equation and attains the step datum strongly in local L¹. The literal vector-test integrals are integrable and include the initial face.

    The statement records elementary connections between states, but does not identify the returned wave profiles with the shocks, rarefactions or contacts witnessing those connections.

    Conditional global energy estimate for a regular solution of a symmetric first-order system.

    This theorem combines the exact global balance, the integrated production bound, and Mathlib's Grönwall inequality. Every analytic assumption used by those steps is a hypothesis: continuity of total energy, local dominated differentiation, pointwise PDE and coefficient regularity, integrable forcing, and compactly supported C¹ flux slices. It does not construct a solution or establish the hypotheses.

  (n : ℕ) [Fact (0 < n)] (Ω : Set ℝ^n) :
  Type

    Operational atlas for the extension construction on a bounded C¹ domain.

    It includes the specific charts and cutoffs needed to build an extension operator by reducing to the half-space construction and summing via a partition of unity.

    This structure is stronger than the geometric predicate that Ω has C¹ boundary; Boundary.Atlas.Geometric.GraphConstruction constructs it from local graph charts.

    Methods

    Ω is open.

    bounded : Bornology.IsBounded Ω

    Ω is bounded.

    N : ℕ

    Number of boundary charts (finite).

    chart : Fin (SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.N Ω) → OpenPartialHomeomorph (ℝ^n) ℝ^n

    Boundary charts (partial homeomorphisms) that flatten Ω to the half-space.

    chart_contDiff : ∀ (i : Fin (SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.N Ω)),
  ContDiff ℝ 1 fun x ↦ ↑(SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.chart i) x

    C¹ regularity of the (total) chart maps.

    We work with charts as total functions ℝ^n → ℝ^n which are C¹ globally, and only later restrict them to an open source where they are invertible.

    The weak chain rule below uses globally defined maps. Obtaining such representatives from the standard local definition of a bounded C¹ boundary requires shrinking the chart neighborhoods.

    chart_symm_contDiff : ∀ (i : Fin (SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas.N Ω)),

    On each chart domain, membership in Ω is equivalent to membership in the upper half-space.

  (hΩV : closure Ω ⊆ V) :
  SobolevSpace.Extension.GraphSpace.SupportedOperator
    n k p Ω V

    Localize a bounded extension of any finite Sobolev order to an arbitrary open neighborhood of closure Ω.

    This gives condition (ii) of Evans §5.4, Theorem 1, "Eu has support within V", which Evans arranges in step 6 of the proof. We choose a smooth cutoff with support in V and equal to one on closure Ω, multiply the original extension by it, and retain both a.e. agreement on Ω and bounded linearity. The domain need only be measurable; the cutoff acts on the whole-space extension. This includes order zero and p = ∞.

    theorem SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.Rellich.baseCoordinateL2_isCompactOperator_of_c1Domain

    SobolevSpace.Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas
      n Ω] :
  IsCompactOperator
    ⇑SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.wkpBaseCoordinateCLM

    Rellich compactness for H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω) under the operational Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas hypothesis. The order-zero inclusion

    H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω)

    is compact when Ω carries the operational chart-and-cutoff data used by the extension theorem. Deriving this hypothesis from the standard assertion that Ω has C¹ boundary is a separate geometric step.

    The proof factors the inclusion in four steps. Extension.C1.extensionCLM sends H¹(Ω) boundedly into H¹(ℝ^n) and agrees with the original base function almost everywhere on Ω. Multiplying by a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one on closure Ω and restricting to a ball B containing its support lands continuously in H¹₀(B). The bounded-domain Rellich theorem for H¹₀(B) makes zero extension followed by the base-coordinate map compact, and precomposition keeps it compact. Finally restriction L²(ℝ^n) → L²(Ω) is bounded, and since the cutoff is one on Ω the composite is the order-zero inclusion.

    structure SobolevSpace.HasWeakDerivativeOn {n : ℕ} (Ω : Set ℝ^n)
  (α : List (Fin n)) (f g : ℝ^n → ℝ) : Prop
    structure SobolevSpace.HasWeakDerivativeOn {n : ℕ}
  (Ω : Set ℝ^n) (α : List (Fin n))
  (f g : ℝ^n → ℝ) : Prop

    A weak-derivative relation on a set Ω, tested against globally smooth functions whose closed support lies in Ω.

    We use Mathlib's test-function type 𝓓((⊤ : Opens (ℝ^n)), ℝ) and require its tsupport (closed support) to lie in Ω. When Ω is open, this is the test class C_c^∞(Ω) of Evans §5.2.1.

    Both f and its proposed weak derivative g are required to lie in L¹_loc(Ω), and the sign is (-1)^|α|, exactly as in Evans §5.2.1, (3). For an arbitrary set the predicate is still a well-formed test-function relation, but it is not automatically the standard Sobolev weak derivative: the test class can be too small (and can be trivial when Ω has empty interior), so uniqueness may fail. Results identifying this relation with the usual weak derivative therefore require openness or another explicit test-function density hypothesis.

    Fields

    locallyIntegrable_f : MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrableOn f Ω MeasureTheory.volume

    The base function belongs to L¹_loc(Ω).

    locallyIntegrable_g : MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrableOn g Ω MeasureTheory.volume

    The proposed weak derivative belongs to L¹_loc(Ω).

    integral_identity : ∀ (φ : TestFunction ⊤ ℝ ⊤),
  tsupport φ.toFun ⊆ Ω →
    ∫ (x : ℝ^n), f x * PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv α φ.toFun x ∂SobolevSpace.domainMeasure n Ω =
      (-1) ^ α.length * ∫ (x : ℝ^n), g x * φ.toFun x ∂SobolevSpace.domainMeasure n Ω

    The distributional integration-by-parts identity.

    structure SobolevSpace.SobolevSpaceOn (n k : ℕ) (p : ENNReal) (Ω : Set ℝ^n) : Type
    structure SobolevSpace.SobolevSpaceOn (n k : ℕ)
  (p : ENNReal) (Ω : Set ℝ^n) : Type

    A representative-level package of Lᵖ functions and weak-derivative witnesses on Ω.

    This stores a concrete representative toFun and existential weak-derivative data. It does not identify functions modulo almost-everywhere equality; use SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.WkpSpaceOn for the Lp-quotient normed-space packaging.

    For 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞ and open Ω, this is the representative-level condition defining W^{k,p}(Ω) in Evans §5.2.2. The order-zero witness is then redundant, but retaining it makes local integrability explicit when this structure is used at other exponents and prevents nonintegrable functions from entering through the totalized Bochner integral. On a nonopen set the structure uses the generalized test-function relation documented by HasWeakDerivativeOn, so the usual uniqueness theorem need not apply.

        k →
      ℝ^n → ENNReal) :
  Prop

    For every realizable weighted graph U and accuracy ε there are: a graph V within ε/3 of U in the w-norm, a bounded reference weight v with a dominated weight q, and a sequence of test functions converging to V in the v-norm whose w-distance to V is eventually at most the q-distance plus ε/3 (EventuallyDistLeWeightedDistAdd).

    All witnesses, including the comparison constants B and C, are chosen per U and ε. Since q = v = 0 and V = U are admissible, the predicate is equivalent to approximation of every realizable weighted graph by eligible test functions in the w-norm, arranged in the shape of the localize-compare-mollify argument.

No row inequality is assumed.

    The hypothesis hradial_axis requires every order-n row, including the pure-axial row ∂_z^n f, to vanish on the axis r = 0. This restricts the theorem to data all of whose order-n rows have zero axis trace: at n = 0 to functions vanishing on the axis, as odd profiles do, and for n ≥ 1 it excludes even profiles whose even-exponent rows need not vanish there.

    Noncompact interpolation for all mixed derivatives of middle order n + 1.

    The pure-axial row uses axial integration by parts; every positive-radial row uses radial integration by parts with its order-n predecessor. The successor identities identify both derivatives without commuting mixed partials. Local C² regularity is required only along these predecessor slices in r > 0, and the middle weight is differentiable there.

    Weighted L² membership supplies the three square integrabilities and weighted measurabilities. The cross-term integrabilities and the two endpoint limits of each boundary product remain explicit. Neither compact support, a zero value trace on the axis, nor any row inequality is assumed.

    Weight comparisons hold almost everywhere for the open-half-plane product measure. Zero extension supplies globally nonnegative weights to the Cauchy estimate without imposing conditions at the singular origin. The conclusion is one adjacent-order interpolation step.

Approximate the compact operator in operator norm by finite-rank maps. Their adjoints are finite-rank and hence compact; preservation of the operator norm by the adjoint and closedness of the compact-operator class pass compactness to the limiting adjoint.

Schauder's theorem for real or complex Hilbert spaces states

K:H_1\to H_2\ \text{compact} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K^*:H_2\to H_1\ \text{compact}.

Here K^* is Mathlib's Hilbert adjoint of the bounded linear map K.

Choose eigenvectors for the distinct eigenvalues and form their increasing finite-dimensional invariant spans. Riesz's lemma supplies uniformly separated vectors in those spans. If the eigenvalues converged to a nonzero limit, compactness of K would give a convergent subsequence after reciprocal rescaling, contradicting the separation estimate.

Let K be compact on a real Hilbert space. If (\lambda_j) is an injective sequence of nonzero real eigenvalues and \lambda_j\to\lambda, then

\lambda=0.

This is the sequential accumulation statement in Evans's compact-spectrum theorem.
Write the nonzero spectrum as the countable union of the finite sets on which the absolute value is at least 1/(k+1).

For a compact operator K, the nonzero real point spectrum

\sigma_{\mathrm p}(K)\setminus\{0\} =\left\{\lambda\ne0:\exists v\ne0,\ Kv=\lambda v\right\}

is countable.

Every eigenvalue lies in the closed interval determined by the operator norm. An infinite set bounded away from zero would therefore have a convergent injective subsequence whose limit is nonzero, contradicting the preceding accumulation theorem.

For every \varepsilon>0, a compact operator K has only finitely many real eigenvalues away from zero:

\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb R: |\lambda|\geq\varepsilon,\ \exists v\ne0,\ Kv=\lambda v\right\} \quad\text{is finite}.

Composing the original weak operator on the left with the shifted inverse gives a compact perturbation of the identity. Closed range and the Hilbert-space range-orthogonality criterion then identify solvability with orthogonality to the adjoint kernel.

Let B:V\times V\to\mathbb R be a continuous weak form that becomes coercive after adding a compact mass term, and let F\in V^*. Then

\bigl[\exists u\in V,\ \forall v\in V,\ B(u,v)=F(v)\bigr] \iff \bigl[\forall w\in V,\ (\forall v\in V,\ B(v,w)=0)\Rightarrow F(w)=0\bigr].

Thus solvability is exactly orthogonality of the load to every homogeneous solution of the adjoint weak problem.

The zero-index theorem gives \dim\ker T=\dim\ker T^*. If the kernel is trivial, bijectivity of the continuous Fredholm map follows from surjectivity (range is closed plus trivial cokernel). If the kernel is nontrivial, uniqueness fails. The two cases are mutually exclusive because a nontrivial kernel element is a nonzero homogeneous solution.

Let V be a real Hilbert space and let B be a bounded bilinear form on V. Suppose there are a real number \lambda and a bounded bilinear form M whose associated operator V\to V^* is compact such that the shifted form B+\lambda M is coercive. Then exactly one of the following branches holds:

\exists u\ne0,\ \forall v,\ B(u,v)=0,

or

\forall F\in V^*,\ \exists!\,u\in V,\ \forall v,\ B(u,v)=F(v).

The two branches are mutually exclusive.

Extend it to a finite-rank operator A:H\to H by first projecting orthogonally onto N. Since M=(\operatorname{range}S)^\perp, the equation (S-A)x=0 forces Sx=Ax=0. Thus x\in N and A_0x=0, so injectivity of A_0 gives x=0.

The operator K+A is compact, so the compact Fredholm alternative makes T=I-(K+A)=S-A surjective. Choose y\in M outside the range of A_0 and solve Tx=y. Then Sx=Ax+y lies in both \operatorname{range}S and M, hence is zero. It follows that x\in N and y=-Ax=A_0(-x), contradicting the choice of y. Therefore \dim M\leq\dim N. Applying the same argument to K^* gives the reverse inequality.

For a compact operator K:H\to H on a real Hilbert space H,

\dim\ker(K-I)=\dim\ker(K^*-I).

Both kernels are finite-dimensional eigenspaces at the nonzero eigenvalue 1. The equality is the index-zero assertion for a compact perturbation of the identity.

Compose the weak operator on the left with the shifted inverse to obtain I-K, with K compact. This preserves the primal kernel. After Riesz identification, the Hilbert-space representative of B factors as T=Q(I-K) with Q invertible. Then T^*=(I-K)^*Q^*, so the invertible map Q^* identifies \ker T^* with \ker((I-K)^*). The compact index-zero theorem gives finiteness and equality of the two nullities.

B_\gamma(u,v)=B(u,v)+\gamma M(u,v).

If B_\gamma is coercive and M is compact, then the primal and adjoint homogeneous spaces

N=\ker B,\qquad N^*=\ker B^*

are finite-dimensional and have equal dimension:

\dim N=\dim N^*<\infty.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open, x_*\in\Omega, and w:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n be C^1 on \Omega. If \det Dw(x_*)\ne0, there are open sets U\subseteq\Omega and V, with x_*\in U and w(x_*)\in V, such that w:U\to V is a homeomorphism with a C^1 inverse X:V\to U. Moreover,

Nonsingularity is assumed at one point; the chart and its regularity on the whole target are conclusions.

the construction gives a local inverse chart and its explicit C^2 dual v, satisfying

The coefficients depend only on the new independent variable p.

\nabla v(p)=X(p),\qquad D^2v(p)=\bigl(D^2u(X(p))\bigr)^{-1} \quad(p\in V).

These are the actual derivatives of u and v.

Hilbert reflexivity identifies the weak space with the range of its canonical weak-star double-dual embedding. Banach–Alaoglu gives compactness of the bounded weak-star closure, and the embedding transfers compactness back to the weak topology. Weak closedness removes the closure operation.

A weakly closed subset of a complete real Hilbert space is weakly compact when its underlying normed-space set is bounded:

K\subset H,\qquad K\ \text{weakly closed and norm bounded} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K\ \text{weakly compact}.

The Lean theorem is stated for Mathlib's weak-space topology and proves topological compactness.

The weak topology on H is the initial topology generated by all continuous linear functionals \ell:H\to\mathbb R. Therefore each evaluation map is continuous by construction. Applying that continuity to x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x gives \ell(x_\alpha)\to\ell(x) for every \ell\in H^*.

Weak convergence in a real normed space gives convergence against each continuous functional:

x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ell(x_\alpha)\longrightarrow\ell(x) \qquad(\ell\in H^*).

Pull a double-dual functional back along the Fréchet–Riesz isometric equivalence between the Hilbert space and its continuous dual. Applying the inverse equivalence produces a vector whose canonical double-dual image is the original functional.

For a complete real Hilbert space H, the canonical isometric map

\iota_H:H\longrightarrow(H^*)^*,\qquad \iota_H(x)(\ell)=\ell(x),

is surjective. Thus H is reflexive in the functional-analytic sense used by the direct method.

Every continuous linear map A_j is continuous from the weak topology of H to the weak topology of K: composing a continuous functional on K with A_j gives a continuous functional on H. Hence each kernel is weakly closed, and arbitrary intersections preserve closedness. A weak limit that is eventually in this intersection remains in it. Finally, intersecting with a weakly closed bounded set preserves closedness and boundedness, so Hilbert weak compactness applies.

Let A_j:H\to K be any family of continuous linear maps. Their simultaneous kernel

\mathcal C=\bigcap_j\ker A_j

is weakly closed. Consequently, if x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x and, eventually, A_jx_\alpha=0 for all j simultaneously, then A_jx=0 for every j. If S\subset H is weakly closed and norm bounded, then S\cap\mathcal C is weakly compact.

The same argument preserves, under weak limits, incompressibility, zero mean, homogeneous traces, and other linear PDE side conditions once the relevant operators are continuous.
