As an example, the affine Euler curve 1+t is compared with the exact trajectory \exp t for u'=u on [0,1]. Its residual is -t, hence has norm at most one, and the generated uniform error is \exp(1)-1. An exact CAS proof or a FloatLib enclosure may supply the residual bound. The ODE stability theorem consumes that real bound and gives the same final ApproxOn statement.

Let L:\mathbb R[X]\to\mathbb R be linear with L(q^2)>0 for every q\ne0. The monic orthogonal polynomial p_n of L is monic of degree n and satisfies L(p_nq)=0 for every q with \deg q<n. It is unique: any monic polynomial of degree n with this property equals p_n. For a weight w continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, the functional p\mapsto\int_a^b p\,w is positive on nonzero squares, and its orthogonal polynomials are the ones used for Gaussian quadrature.

The divisor statement is the sign argument for \int_a^b q\,r^2w. An irreducible real factor of degree two has no real root, so it cannot divide p, and p splits. If q^2 divides p with q nonconstant, write p=q^2r; then L((qr)^2)=L(p\,r)=0, contradicting positivity, so p is squarefree. A root at the endpoint a would give p=(x-a)r with \int_a^b(x-a)\,r^2w=0, but (x-a)w is a weight that is positive on the interior; the endpoint b is symmetric. A monic squarefree polynomial that splits is the product of x-x_i over its distinct roots.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, and let p\ne0 be orthogonal against w to every polynomial of lower degree. Then every nonconstant divisor of p has a root in [a,b], p is squarefree and splits over \mathbb R, and every root of p lies in the open interval (a,b). Consequently the monic orthogonal polynomial p_n has exactly n distinct real roots, all in (a,b), and they can be listed as x_0,\dots,x_{n-1} so that the nodal polynomial \prod_i(x-x_i) equals p_n.

A verified panel evaluator, checked variable boxes, and a proof of successful evaluation define a total range provider for one symbolic expression. The provider stores the returned backend interval together with its direct enclosure theorem.

For every a<b with [a,b]\subseteq s, its total contract is

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \operatorname{eval}(e,x)\in\operatorname{result}(a,b).

The ceiling gives N\ge(B/\varepsilon)^{1/m}, and raising both sides to the power m gives N^m\ge B/\varepsilon. The composite budget is B/N^m, and certificate soundness bounds the actual error by the budget.

Let m\ne0, D>0, a\le b, C\ge0 and \varepsilon>0, put B=C(b-a)^{m+1}/D, and let N=\max(1,\lceil(B/\varepsilon)^{1/m}\rceil). Then B/N^m\le\varepsilon. Consequently, for a panel rule of order m, an integrand in C^m[a,b], a<b, and a derivative bounder whose bound on every subinterval is at most C, the composite certificate on the planned mesh has error budget at most \varepsilon, and its value is within \varepsilon of \int_a^bf.

A panel rule of order m is a normalized rule Q with a positive constant D and a proof that, on every ordered interval [a,b], every f\in C^m[a,b] with \|f^{(m)}\|\le M there satisfies \|\int_a^b f-Q(f)\|\le M(b-a)^{m+1}/D. Its composite certificate on N>0 equal panels, given a panelwise derivative bounder with common bound C, has error budget C(b-a)^{m+1}/(DN^m). Simpson's rule and the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule are panel rules of order four.

Structural induction on the expression constructs its Fréchet derivative using the analytic sum, product, quotient, power, and elementary chain rules. The validity hypotheses discharge each rule's domain conditions. Evaluating the resulting continuous linear map on e_i gives exactly the evaluated symbolic derivative, hence the stated coordinate identity.

At every point satisfying the generated validity conditions, symbolic differentiation in coordinate i agrees with our analytic Euclidean partial derivative: (\operatorname{diff}_i e)^\sharp(x)=\partial_i(e^\sharp)(x).

Fix a point in the global domain and use the cover property to choose a patch containing it. The local certificate on that patch proves the desired predicate at the point. Since the argument is independent of the selected patch, it assembles the local soundness fields into the global theorem.

Patch covers assemble local approximation or residual proofs into a global theorem on the covered domain. The atlas layer, used near singularities or across piecewise regimes, rests on this theorem.

The shared logical contract is

\left(\forall x\in s,\ \exists i,\ x\in s_i\right) \land \left(\forall i,\ \forall x\in s_i,\ P(x)\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in s,\ P(x).

For approximation and residual atlases, P(x) is the corresponding stored norm bound.

Normalize each reflected residual, rewrite its differentiated components using Theorem 10.20, and identify the transport term with Theorem 10.21. The remaining sums and products evaluate definitionally.

For momentum component i, assume ValidAt at x for u_i and p. The Navier–Stokes bridge also assumes validity of every first symbolic partial of u_i; the conservation bridge assumes validity of every flux component. These give the stationary Euler and Navier–Stokes momentum residuals and the divergence-form conservation residual. Incompressibility is a separate equation. The undifferentiated viscosity and source terms need no validity hypotheses for these identities. Componentwise, the Euler bridge gives R_i^{E}(x)=\sum_j u_j(x)\partial_j u_i(x)+\partial_i p(x)-f_i(x), while the Navier–Stokes bridge adds -\nu(x)\Delta u_i(x) and the conservation bridge gives R^{C}(x)=\sum_i\partial_i F_i(x)-f(x).

Here u_t=4, u_{xx}=2, and u_{yy}=2, so the checked residual is 4-2-2=0. Polynomial evaluation and its derivatives are valid everywhere; the coordinate and fixed-time slice bridges therefore apply on all spacetime.

The polynomial profile

u(t,x,y)=x^2+y^2+4t

has zero residual for the ordinary two-dimensional heat-equation problem on all spacetime; the linked SatisfiesPDEProblem theorem is exactly that residual property.

Termwise evaluation encloses each monomial with interval multiplication and natural powers and combines the terms with interval addition. The basic interval operations preserve membership, so induction over the sparse term list shows that the real polynomial value lies between the computed rational endpoints. For the centred form, write p(x)=\sum_k c_k(x-m)^k with the exact shifted coefficients c_k, where m is the midpoint and r the radius of the panel. Since |x-m|\le r, an even power (x-m)^k lies in [0,r^k] and an odd one in [-r^k,r^k], so every term lies in a rational interval and their sum encloses p(x). The enclosure returns one of these two sound intervals.

Exact interval evaluation encloses the value of a sparse rational polynomial at every real point of a rational panel. The root checks first try the centred form, the exact Taylor shift of the polynomial to the midpoint of the panel bounded term by term over its radius, and use termwise evaluation when the centred interval does not exclude zero. This theorem is the semantic basis for both root exclusion and derivative-sign checks.

x\in[a,b] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(x)\in\operatorname{enclosure}(p,[a,b]).

Expand a polynomial of degree at most d in the monomial basis. Linearity of both integration and the weighted rule reduces exactness to each monomial, where it is exactly the assumed moment identity. Affine substitution transports the normalized-interval result to any oriented interval.

If a normalized rule has the exact moments through degree d, it exactly integrates every real polynomial of degree at most d. Affine transport preserves this conclusion on arbitrary oriented intervals. Both the three-node Simpson rule and the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule have the exact moments through degree three, hence exactly integrate every cubic and generate zero-error QuadratureCerts.

Exactness on constants makes the weights of Q_n sum to \int_a^b w. If a polynomial p of degree at most d_n is within \delta of f on [a,b], positivity bounds |Q_n(f)-Q_n(p)| by \delta\int_a^b w, and |\int_a^b (p-f)w| is at most \delta\int_a^b|w|. Since Q_n(p) is the integral of p w, the error on f is at most \delta(\int_a^b w+\int_a^b|w|), a bound independent of n. The Weierstrass theorem supplies p for every \delta>0, and d_n\to\infty makes p admissible for all large n.

Let w be continuous on [a,b] and let Q_n be rules with nonnegative weights and nodes in [a,b], where Q_n integrates every polynomial of degree at most d_n exactly against w and d_n\to\infty. Then Q_n(f)\to\int_a^b f\,w for every f continuous on [a,b]. This is the theorem of Pólya and Steklov. The same statement holds for normalized rules with nonnegative weights transported to [a,b].

A Precision value bundles three requests for FloatLib-backed elementary ranges and a depth for checked box refinement:

(\mathrm{expOrder},\ \mathrm{sqrtDigits},\ \mathrm{logTerms},\ \mathrm{depth}) \quad\text{with defaults}\quad(8,\ 12,\ 10,\ 2).

expOrder supplies FloatLib's exponential degree after promotion of zero to one. sqrtDigits sets the binary grid for the denominator-scaled square-root bounds. logTerms maps to FloatLib degree 2\max(\mathrm{logTerms},1). The sine, cosine, and arctangent adapters use their own fixed parameters. The configuration group (prec := n) sets the first three fields to n; (depth := n) sets the subdivision depth. An omitted policy uses the defaults.

The policy is planner data. Every range theorem holds for all parameter values, so changing the policy preserves soundness while affecting cost and potential sharpness. The final width also depends on input variation, dependence between subexpressions, and period uncertainty, any of which can dominate the error.

Finite search returns a key only together with evidence that the family's acceptance predicate holds for that key. The policy theorem converts this evidence into the requested tolerance bound, and the candidate's stored quadrature soundness identifies the quantity being bounded. A failed search has no conclusion to prove.

A candidate family associates mesh, rule, or arithmetic-schedule keys with ordinary quadrature certificates and an executable Boolean acceptance test. The policy proves that every accepted result meets the requested tolerance. Finite search returns the first accepted key together with that theorem, or none if every candidate fails.

If finite search returns an accepted key k, its projection proves

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -\operatorname{candidate}(k).\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

A quadrature certificate stores a proposed value of a Bochner interval integral, an explicit error budget, and a proof of the corresponding norm estimate. The certificate is indexed by the ordinary Lean integrand and endpoints, so no symbolic expression type appears in theorem statements.

Its trusted field is

q.\mathrm{sound}:\qquad \left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-q.\mathrm{value}\right\| \leq q.\mathrm{error}.

Insert and subtract the exact certificate value Q. The triangle inequality bounds the new integral error by the original quadrature error plus \lVert Q-\widehat Q\rVert; applying the two stored bounds yields E+\delta.

An independently certified numerical value may replace the exact-real quadrature value. Its roundoff bound is added to the analytic quadrature error by the triangle inequality. The theorem is the common interface for a verified exact, interval, or floating-point implementation: a backend must prove the displayed norm bound before its computed value enters the quadrature certificate.

Concretely, if Q is the value stored in a certificate with error E and \widehat Q is a computed replacement satisfying \lVert Q-\widehat Q\rVert\leq\delta, then

\left\lVert\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\widehat Q\right\rVert \leq E+\delta.

At every node, the sample difference is at most \varepsilon. Apply the triangle inequality to the weighted sum, bound each term by |w_j|\varepsilon, and sum to obtain V\varepsilon on the normalized interval. Affine transport contributes the factor |b-a|.

If two scalar integrands differ uniformly by \varepsilon on [[a,b]], their values under a normalized rule differ by at most |b-a|\,V\varepsilon, where V is the sum of the absolute rule weights. This estimate lets a rule that is exact on a nearby model be evaluated on the original integrand while accounting separately for integral-model error and sample-value perturbation.

The quadrature specialization stores accepted local QuadratureCerts in the same backend-independent tree used by real-valued adaptive search. Local interval-integrability evidence justifies composing adjacent panel integrals. Both an over-budget root and a missing root candidate may therefore be recovered by proved child certificates, while a failed finite search returns none.

On success it returns exactly the root theorem

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right|\leq(\tau:\mathbb R),

where a, b, and \tau are the input rationals cast to reals.

The generic rational adaptive kernel keeps endpoints, midpoints, and local tolerances exact. A rejected or unavailable parent candidate is bisected at its rational midpoint; accepted children are combined only through the client's proved error-subadditivity theorem.

The dependent result type records the invariant

\operatorname{searchPartial}(\ldots,\tau)=\operatorname{some}(R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{error}(R.\mathrm{result})\leq(\tau:\mathbb R).

The candidate's proof bounds its semantic real error by the cast of its exact rational budget. Boolean acceptance is precisely the decidable rational comparison of that budget with \tau. Casting this comparison to the reals and composing the inequalities proves the result.

A rational-budget candidate contains a client result, an exact rational upper bound for its semantic error, and a proof relating the two. When decidable rational comparison accepts the candidate, its real error is at most the requested rational tolerance.

Precisely,

\operatorname{accepted}(c,\tau)=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{error}(c.\mathrm{cert})\leq(\tau:\mathbb R).

Polynomial gcd cancellation proposes the reduced rational expression, but the exact normalizer proves the cross-multiplied identity. Checked interval facts then show that every cancelled denominator is nonzero throughout the panel. Substituting those side facts into the conditional normalization theorem gives the pointwise equality used by the derivative bounder.

The rational route proposes a polynomial-gcd cancellation, checks its semantic equality through the exact normalizer, and turns generated denominator conditions into interval obligations. Exact rational hulls cover arbitrary real panels, and checked zero exclusion or an absolute lower bound discharges the nonzero conditions on the whole declared domain.

Writing the checked route as \operatorname{route}(d)=(r,S), its semantic boundary is the conditional identity

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(d,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(r,\rho).

The interval phase proves the premise uniformly on the panel.

Mathlib's Nat.lt_pow_nthRoot_add_one says that one more than the integer fourth root of \lceil B/\tau\rceil has fourth power above it, so the chosen natural's fourth power is at least the exact rational ratio. Rearranging with \tau>0 gives the same tolerance estimate as the real planner.

For exact rational error data, the executable planner rounds B/\mathrm{tolerance} upward and takes one more than the integer fourth root of the result (Mathlib's Nat.nthRoot 4). The resulting positive natural panel count satisfies the same fourth-order inequality without evaluating a noncomputable real root.

Prove the rational evaluator correct by structural induction on the algebraic expression, rejecting precisely the division cases with zero denominator. Apply that equality at each rational quadrature node. Casting commutes with the finite products and sum, so the compiled ordered table has the same real weighted value as the analytic rule.

The rational algebraic fragment of the shared expression language has a fail-closed exact evaluator. Every successful result is proved equal to the existing real expression semantics. A quadrature rule with rational weights and nodes can therefore sample a symbolic integrand exactly, preserve the ordered rule schedule, and cast term-for-term to the existing transported QuadratureRule. Transcendental nodes, malformed literals, and sampled zero denominators are rejected. Optional finite-precision backends consume the exact table through the same interval and weighted-sum interfaces.

At the expression boundary,

\operatorname{evalRat?}(e,\rho)=\operatorname{some}(q) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho_{\mathbb R})=(q:\mathbb R).

For a successfully compiled rule, casting every rational term preserves the analytic schedule and value:

\operatorname{cast}\!\left(\sum_j w_j e(x_j)\right) =\sum_j (w_j:\mathbb R)\, \operatorname{eval}(e,(x_j:\mathbb R)).

Map every rational source node and weight by the affine panel formula and cast the result to the reals. Field identities show term by term that the cast node and weight equal those of the analytic transported rule. Mapping this equality over panels and flattening proves equality of both schedules and values.

Every normalized exact-rational rule compiles uniformly to N > 0 panels by mapping a source term (w,\xi) on panel k to (w/N,(k+\xi)/N). The cast rule is proved equal term-for-term to the canonical analytic uniform-composite list. This preserves both the exact-real value and the panel-major accumulation schedule used by verified numerical backends.

If B<0 the bound holds for every N. Otherwise the ceiling construction gives N\geq(B/\tau)^{1/4} and N\geq1. Positivity permits raising the first inequality to the fourth power, yielding N^4\geq B/\tau. Rearranging with \tau>0 proves B/N^4\leq\tau.

Let B=C(b-a)^5/D. For a positive tolerance, choosing N=\max(1,\lceil(B/\mathrm{tolerance})^{1/4}\rceil) proves B/N^4\leq\mathrm{tolerance}. This is the case m=4 of the planner for an error model B/N^m of any order m>0, and it is the rule-independent planner behind every fourth-order uniform composite rule.

Each local rewrite uses the corresponding identity for real powers, square roots, or exponentials under its recorded positivity conditions. The bottom-up traversal retains every condition from the rewrites it applies. Induction over the traversal composes the local evaluation equalities into the equality for the whole tree; when the expression contains no power atom the pass returns it unchanged.

The side-conditioned pipeline contains a pass for the algebra of real powers and of the exponential, which it treats as the power of \mathrm e. Inside a product or quotient all powers of one base collect into a single power, nested powers flatten, powers of products distribute, exponents are put into a polynomial normal form, and a literal exponent is read back as a natural power, a reciprocal, or a square root. Each rewrite that Mathlib states for a positive base records the positivity of that base as a condition unless the base is structurally positive (a positive numeral, \pi, \mathrm e, an exponential, or a product of these); rewrites valid for the total Real.rpow, and the exponential identities, record nothing.

Writing (e',S) for the output of the pass on e,

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e',\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(e,\rho).

Structural induction on the expression. Constants and coordinate projections are smooth; sums, products, and negations preserve ContDiffAt; quotients, logarithms, square roots, real powers, and the inverse sine and cosine are smooth at every point satisfying the validity clause of their constructor, by Mathlib's ContDiffAt lemmas for the elementary functions and the field operations; the remaining elementary functions are smooth everywhere. The derivative bridge also gives differentiability, and the set and global forms quantify these pointwise statements over their domain.

The validity predicate that justifies one symbolic derivative also certifies regularity of every order. At a point where ValidAt holds, evaluation of a reflected expression is C^m for every smoothness order m, the analytic order included, because each constructor is interpreted by an elementary function that Mathlib proves smooth of every order away from its singularities; the On and global forms assume validity at every point of the set or the space. The theorems are stated for the two conventions of the theorem-facing tactics, functions on \mathbb R^n and functions on \mathbb R with frozen parameters, and they are what cas applies to a DifferentiableAt, Differentiable, ContDiffAt, ContDiffOn, or ContDiff goal:

\operatorname{ValidAt}(x,e) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^\sharp\text{ is }C^m\text{ at }x \qquad\text{for every }m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,\infty,\omega\}.

Rewrite the analytic residual as the evaluation of the lowered residual, using the analytic side conditions. ClosedResidualVanishesAt is exactly the assertion that this evaluation is zero, so it finishes the proof. A side-aware normalizer is one way to supply that vanishing proof after its denominator and branch conditions have been discharged.

In positive dimension, lower a differential equation against a closed-form ansatz to a symbolic residual. If that residual evaluates to zero at the point and its analytic side conditions hold there, then R_{\mathrm{closed}}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ R_{\mathrm{analytic}}(u^\sharp,x)=0.

A pointwise residual energy is the square of a LinearPDE's totalized residual expression. A sampled loss sums these energies over a finite list of points. Interpreting this objective as a classical PDE loss requires a separate regularity proof for the candidate field. Given a parameterized model \theta \mapsto u_\theta, its objective is the ordinary composition \theta \mapsto \operatorname{sampledLoss}(u_\theta).

The checked derivative bridge computes the four coordinate derivatives of (-y,x) as 0,-1,1,0. Each symmetric-gradient entry therefore vanishes, so the sum of their squares is pointwise zero. Integral congruence gives the result on every set.

For the planar rigid rotation u(x,y)=(-y,x), every entry of the symmetric gradient vanishes. Consequently its small-strain energy density integrates to zero on every domain. The public theorem is an ordinary integral identity; the symbolic engine is used only to calculate the coordinate derivatives and close the pointwise algebra.

Take a root in the covered domain and choose an atlas panel containing it. A root-free panel is impossible because its certificate excludes zero. Consequently the chosen panel is one of the root regions, which proves the covering conclusion. The global version first uses the outer bound to place the root in the covered domain.

A root atlas combines root-free and uniquely rooted panels with a proved cover. Every real root in the outer domain therefore belongs to one of the atlas's isolated root regions.

If \mathcal A is an atlas over D, its projection is

x\in D\land p(x)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists R\in\mathcal A.\mathrm{rootRegions},\ x\in R.

For a global atlas the premise x\in D is removed by its outer-root bound.
Sound interval evaluation places every p(x) in the computed range. The Boolean root-free test proves that zero is outside that range. Therefore no enclosed value can equal zero.

If checked interval evaluation excludes zero, the polynomial is nonzero throughout the panel. The result can be used directly as a side condition for an ordinary real-expression theorem.

\operatorname{rootFree}(p,[a,b])=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in[a,b],\ p(x)\neq0.

Two integrations by parts write each error as \int_a^bK(t)f''(t)\,dt. For the trapezoid rule the kernel is (t-a)(b-t)/2\ge0, of mass (b-a)^3/12. For the midpoint rule it is (t-a)^2/2 on the left half and (b-t)^2/2 on the right, of mass (b-a)^3/24. Bound f'' by C.

On an ordered interval, for f\in C^2[a,b] with \|f''\|\le C there,

\left\|\int_a^bf-\frac{b-a}2\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr)\right\| \le\frac{C(b-a)^3}{12},\qquad \left\|\int_a^bf-(b-a)f\!\left(\tfrac{a+b}2\right)\right\| \le\frac{C(b-a)^3}{24}.

Both rules are exact through degree one, and they are panel rules of order two with D=12 and D=24.

For each splittable coordinate x_i, the planner encloses the symbolic partial derivative and assigns the exact rational score

(b_i-a_i)\max\{|L_i|,|U_i|\}, \qquad \operatorname{eval}(\operatorname{diff}_i e,X)\subseteq[L_i,U_i].

This is an enclosure of the formal derivative expression. Its identification with an analytic partial derivative requires the separate validity hypotheses. The largest positive score selects the coordinate; if no score is positive, the widest coordinate with an unenclosed derivative is chosen. The ranking is a heuristic, and soundness comes from the checked interval enclosures used by the adaptive search.

Every checked symbolic transformation is recorded by one route type. A SideClaimRoute stores the source and target expressions, the list of expressions that must not vanish, and a proof that the target and source evaluate equally wherever that list holds; a positivity requirement is encoded as the nonvanishing of a square root. An unconditional transformation is the same object with an empty list of assumptions.

For a route with source l, target r, and assumption list S,

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(r,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(l,\rho), \qquad S=[\,]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall\rho,\ \operatorname{eval}(r,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(l,\rho).

Side-aware constructors consume a checked equality route together with proofs of every emitted nonzero condition. The rational specialization may cancel polynomial factors, but its simplified derivative enters the bounder only through that conditional semantic equality.

The constructor composes

\left(\forall x\in[a,b],\operatorname{SideHolds}(x,S)\right) \land \left(\forall x\in[a,b],|\operatorname{eval}(r,x)|\leq B\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in[a,b],\|f^{(n)}(x)\|\leq B.

The side-aware route proves evaluation preservation conditionally on every emitted nonzero or branch requirement. Once SideHolds supplies those requirements, the route's final zero expression evaluates to zero, so the original expression does as well.

Rational cancellation and other conditional rewrites return the nonzero conditions they require. Under those conditions, reduction to zero again implies equality of the original real expression.

If normalization returns a zero expression together with side conditions S, then

\operatorname{normalizeWithSide}(e)=(0,S) \land\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)=0.

Apply the rational fourth-order planner with denominator 2880, the error constant B=C(b-a)^5/2880 of the composite Simpson theorem: its panel count N satisfies B/N^4\leq\tau in exact rational arithmetic.

Substituting the sharp Simpson denominator D=2880 into the executable rational planner produces a panel count whose composite error bound C(b-a)^5/(2880N^4) is at most the requested rational tolerance.

Represent the Simpson error as the integral of the fourth derivative against its Peano kernel, whose two polynomial pieces live on [a,(a+b)/2] and [(a+b)/2,b]; four integrations by parts produce it, and cubic exactness cancels all boundary polynomial terms. The kernel has fixed sign and exact mass (b-a)^5/2880. Bounding the fourth derivative by C gives the stated norm estimate.

For an ordered interval [a,b], a C^4 scalar integrand, and a bound C on its fourth within-derivative, the Peano-kernel argument gives the classical one-panel Simpson estimate \lVert\int_a^b f-S(f)\rVert\le C(b-a)^5/2880, returned as a QuadratureCert.

FloatLib proves both containment and the width bound for its integer-root enclosure. Since d>0, division by d preserves the endpoint order, and \sqrt{qd^2}=d\sqrt q gives the desired point enclosure. For negative arguments, Mathlib's square root is zero. Apply monotonicity of this total function to the two endpoint certificates to enclose the full panel.

For every rational panel and every binary precision s, sqrtRangeInterval contains Mathlib's total real square root throughout the panel. At a nonnegative endpoint q=n/d in lowest terms, the point enclosure has width at most 1/(d2^s) and is exact when its lower endpoint squares to q. Negative endpoints map to zero. The default precision is 12 binary digits.

The checked division identities certify the gcd decomposition used by the square-free reduction. They show that removing repeated factors preserves exactly the zero set. Coprimality of the reduced polynomial and its derivative then rules out a point where both vanish, so every remaining root is simple.

A radical certificate proves that a proposed square-free reduction has exactly the same real zero set as the original polynomial and has nonzero derivative at every root. The executable Yun-style generator returns only a certificate that passes the independent check of two divisibility identities and a Bézout identity.

Writing the checked radical as r,

\forall x\in\mathbb R,\qquad p(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow r(x)=0, \qquad r(x)=0\Longrightarrow r'(x)\neq0.

A signed Euclidean chain is proposed outside the checker and accepted only when the independent structural checker SturmCertificate.valid accepts every initial, recurrence, degree, and terminal condition. SymLean has no chain generator: a caller supplies the chain.

\mathrm{valid}(p, C)=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C\text{ is a validated Sturm certificate for }p.

The independent checker verifies the first two entries and every signed quotient-remainder identity using exact polynomial normalization. At the terminal entry it checks a zero formal derivative and a nonzero value at zero. The mean value theorem makes that polynomial constant, hence nowhere zero. Collecting these checked equalities yields the defining Sturm-chain conditions.

An accepted Sturm certificate begins with the requested polynomial and its formal derivative, satisfies every signed Euclidean recurrence exactly, and ends in a polynomial that is nonzero on the real line. These are structural facts about the checked chain, before any root-counting theorem is applied.

For a chain S_0,\ldots,S_m, validation establishes

S_0=p,\qquad S_1=p',\qquad S_{i-1}=Q_iS_i-S_{i+1},\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R,\ S_m(x)\neq0.

Apply the Sturm count theorem at every node. A node of count zero is root-free; a node of count one contains a root and cannot contain two distinct roots. For a split node, additivity of root counts over its adjacent children preserves the parent's exact count. Structural induction over the accepted subdivision tree therefore produces the root atlas.

Sturm counts certify unique-root intervals and exact root counts for a checked subdivision tree. An accepted finite subdivision therefore projects to the same root-atlas interface used by interval and monotonicity certificates.

For each accepted node N with interval I_N,

N.\mathrm{rootCount} =\#\{x\in I_N^\circ\mid p(x)=0\},

and every leaf with count one projects to an \exists!\,x\in I_N,\ p(x)=0 certificate.

Along an interval containing no endpoint root, sign variation is locally constant except when crossing a root of p. The signed Euclidean recurrence shows that noninitial chain entries cannot create a net jump, while each distinct root of p decreases the variation by one. Summing the jumps from a to b gives the root count.

For an accepted chain and ordered rational endpoints that are not roots, the drop in endpoint sign variations equals the number of distinct real roots in the intervening open interval. This is the analytic Sturm theorem that gives the executable variation count its mathematical meaning.

V(a)-V(b) =\#\{x\in(a,b)\mid p(x)=0\}.

Subtract the two finite power series term by term and apply the triangle inequality. Each coefficient difference is at most \delta_k, while |x-a|^k\leq(b-a)^k on the ordered interval. Summing these bounds gives the displayed perturbation estimate.

Suppose the stored coefficient c_k is within \delta_k\geq0 of the exact Taylor coefficient c_k^\ast for 0\leq k\leq n. For the stored jet q_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k, the coefficient bounds imply

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left|T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f(x)-q_n(x)\right| \leq\sum_{k=0}^{n}\delta_k(b-a)^k.

This estimate contains coefficient uncertainty only.

FloatLib identifies its rational Taylor sum and error radius with their real counterparts, then applies Mathlib's Real.exp_bound with d+1 terms. The hypothesis |q|\leq1 gives the bound |\exp q-T_n(q)|\leq R_n(q). Its contains_expSmall theorem expresses that absolute-error estimate as interval containment. CEGA reuses the upstream kernel through its exponential range adapter.

For every rational q with |q|\leq1 and every degree d, FloatLib's expSmall q d encloses \exp q. With n=d+1, the polynomial T_n(q) has absolute error at most R_n(q), so the real exponential lies between the exact rational endpoints T_n(q)-R_n(q) and T_n(q)+R_n(q).

Insert the exact Taylor polynomial between f and the stored jet q_n. The Taylor remainder theorem bounds the first difference, and the coefficient perturbation theorem bounds the second. The triangle inequality adds these two independent budgets, producing the certificate's soundness field.

The combined certificate converts derivative enclosures into coefficient centers c_k, coefficient radii \delta_k, and a bound C on the (n+1)-st within derivative. For q_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k, its soundness theorem is

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad |f(x)-q_n(x)| \leq C\frac{(b-a)^{n+1}}{n!} +\sum_{k=0}^{n}\delta_k(b-a)^k.

The same proposition is exported as an ordinary ModelApproxCert. Runtime roundoff in evaluating q_n is a separate error.

Expand the finite real jet as its coefficient sum and substitute the definition c_k=D^k_{[a,b]}f(a)/k!. The resulting finite sum is exactly the definition of Mathlib's scalar Taylor evaluation, so the two functions agree for every x.

Let c_k=(k!)^{-1}D^k_{[a,b]}f(a) be the exact within-derivative coefficient. For every real x, evaluating the finite power-basis jet gives exactly Mathlib's scalar Taylor polynomial:

\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k =T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f(x).

Thus the finite coefficient sum and the analytic object used by the remainder theorem have the same real semantics.

For a multi-index \alpha:\iota\to_0\mathbb N, an order-N jet is a formal coefficient family J_\alpha. When a separate semantic theorem identifies these coefficients with derivatives, the normalization convention is

J_\alpha(f,x)=\frac{D^\alpha f(x)}{\alpha!}.

Formal products use ordinary power-series convolution:

(JK)_\alpha =\sum_{\beta+\gamma=\alpha}J_\beta K_\gamma.

The order index controls finite extraction and finite formal composition. The underlying representation is a full formal power series: coefficients above the index may be nonzero, and the carrier itself contains no function, base point, differentiability proof, or convergence theorem.

The leaf construction combines the checked symbolic derivative pipeline with a noncomputable Taylor polynomial. Given rational a<b, regularity through order n+1, and a proved nonnegative rational bound \lVert D^{n+1}_{[a,b]}f(x)\rVert\leq C, a successful leaf construction returns the exact Taylor model T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f with

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left|f(x)-T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f(x)\right| \leq C\frac{(b-a)^{n+1}}{n!}.

The compiler records analytic branch conditions explicitly and verifies rational cancellation and denominator conditions. Unsupported derivatives or failed interval obligations return none, so this theorem is exposed only after all required evidence has been constructed.

Apply the within-interval Taylor remainder theorem at the left endpoint. The supplied uniform bound on the next derivative controls the remainder factor, and |x-a|\leq b-a makes the estimate uniform over the panel.

A uniform bound on the (n+1)-st within derivative, together with the certificate's C^{n+1} regularity on the ordered interval, gives the analytic remainder between the source function and its exact Taylor polynomial. This term contains no coefficient uncertainty and no runtime roundoff.

The right side is monic of degree n+2. It is orthogonal to p_{n+1} by the choice of \alpha_{n+1}, to p_n by the choice of \beta_n, and to every polynomial of degree below n because L(xp_{n+1}p_k)=0 for k<n. Uniqueness identifies it with p_{n+2}. For the second formula, xp_n-p_{n+1} has degree at most n, so orthogonality of p_{n+1} gives L(xp_{n+1}p_n)=L(p_{n+1}^2).

With \alpha_n=L(xp_n^2)/L(p_n^2) and \beta_n=L(xp_{n+1}p_n)/L(p_n^2), the monic orthogonal polynomials of L satisfy p_0=1, p_1=x-\alpha_0, and

p_{n+2}=(x-\alpha_{n+1})\,p_{n+1}-\beta_n\,p_n\qquad(n\ge0).

Moreover \beta_n=L(p_{n+1}^2)/L(p_n^2), so \beta_n>0.

The ceiling square-root choice ensures N^2\geq B/\tau and N>0. Rearranging gives B/N^2\leq\tau; substituting the trapezoidal error constant B=|b-a|^3\zeta/12 into the composite trapezoidal certificate proves the result.

Under these same regularity and derivative-bound hypotheses, for a positive tolerance the checked planner chooses N=\max(1,\lceil\sqrt{B/\mathrm{tolerance}}\rceil) with B=|b-a|^3\zeta/12. The bound forces \zeta\ge 0, and the resulting composite trapezoidal certificate has error at most the requested tolerance. The square-root choice retains the standard O(\mathrm{tolerance}^{-1/2}) mesh scaling.

Reserve the interval radius r for replacement error and invoke the trapezoidal planner with the positive remaining budget \tau-r. The roundoff-replacement theorem adds the two contributions, and (\tau-r)+r=\tau gives the requested total bound.

Under the trapezoidal regularity and second-derivative-bound hypotheses, one user-supplied tolerance can control analytic truncation and verified numerical error. Let I have radius r<\mathrm{tolerance}. The enclosure proof must refer to the exact-real trapezoidal value on the mesh planned with the budget \mathrm{tolerance}-r. Replacing that exact rule value by the interval midpoint then has total certified error at most the original tolerance.

Mathlib's composite trapezoidal rule is exposed through the common certificate interface. Assume f is C^2 on S=[\min(a,b),\max(a,b)] and |D^2_S f(x)|\leq\zeta for every real x, where D^2_S denotes the second iterated within-derivative. For N>0 subintervals the error is at most |b-a|^3\zeta/(12N^2).

Split the interval into N equal panels and add the local integral identities. The triangle inequality sums the local errors. Since each panel has length (b-a)/N, the sum of N terms C((b-a)/N)^5/D simplifies to C(b-a)^5/(DN^4). Flattening the panel term lists preserves the same finite weighted sum.

Any local quadrature constructor with certified error C(v-u)^5/D can be accumulated over N>0 equal panels. The generic theorem produces error C(b-a)^5/(DN^4) and a canonical flattened ordered term list whose exact weighted sum equals the composite value. Smoothness is assumed only on the root interval, and one IteratedDerivativeBounderOn supplies each panel's within-derivative bound together with a common upper bound C. Analytic composition and finite-precision execution therefore share one rule-independent boundary.

Continuity and the weak endpoint inequalities give existence by the intermediate value theorem. The derivative enclosure has one strict sign on the whole panel, so the mean value theorem makes p strictly monotone there. A strictly monotone function has at most one zero, proving uniqueness.

Endpoint values satisfying p(a)\le0\le p(b), or the reversed inequalities, give a root by the intermediate value theorem. A checked strict derivative sign makes the polynomial strictly monotone in the corresponding direction. Together they prove that the rational bracket contains exactly one real root, possibly at an endpoint.

For every valid bracket certificate,

\exists!\,x\in[a,b],\qquad p(x)=0.

Induct along the branch selected by the point. At a leaf, the stored validation field proves R(c,d). At a split m, use the left child when x\leq m and the right child otherwise; root membership gives membership in that chosen child, so its induction hypothesis applies. A queried split point uses the left branch. The global approximation estimate is inherited from the erased model tree.

Let R(c,d) be a declared relation between a leaf certificate and its payload. If every leaf satisfies R, then point selection proves

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad R\!\left(c_{\ell_x},d_{\ell_x}\right).

Validated adaptive search preserves this local relation together with the global guarantee \forall x\in[a,b],\ |f(x)-P_\tau(x)|\leq\eta for the requested tolerance \eta.

When the compiled derivative contains no occurrence of the interval variable, one verified evaluation at an enclosure of zero supplies the same bound on every real panel. This avoids asking a finite interval backend to represent arbitrary real endpoints for a constant expression.

Variable independence gives

x\notin\operatorname{vars}(d) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(d,\rho[x\mapsto t]) =\operatorname{eval}(d,\rho[x\mapsto0])

for every t; a single enclosure of the right-hand side is therefore valid on every requested panel.

For each coordinate, Theorem 10.18 identifies evaluation of the reflected partial derivative with the corresponding analytic derivative. The reflected gradient is the vector of these coordinates, divergence is their finite sum, the Laplacian is the sum of the diagonal second derivatives, and curl is the stated alternating combination. Function extensionality and finite-sum congruence assemble the coordinate identities into the four displayed operator identities.

For the Laplacian, applying the first-derivative identity only at x would not suffice: two functions can agree at one point and have different derivatives there. Validity persists on a neighborhood of x, so the analytic first partial and the evaluated symbolic first partial agree throughout that neighborhood. Their derivatives at x therefore agree. Validity of the first symbolic partial justifies the second application of the derivative bridge. These are sufficient conditions on the intermediate formulas; the largest domain of smoothness can be bigger.

At a point where the scalar inputs being differentiated are valid, the coordinatewise bridge gives gradient, divergence, and three-dimensional curl formulas. The Laplacian bridge additionally assumes validity of every first symbolic partial at that point. Hessians, Jacobians, symmetric gradients, tensor divergence, and vector Laplacians use the same finite-indexed construction. In particular, (\nabla_{\mathrm{sym}}e)^\sharp(x)=\nabla(e^\sharp)(x), (\Delta_{\mathrm{sym}}e)^\sharp(x)=\Delta(e^\sharp)(x), (\operatorname{div}_{\mathrm{sym}}F)^\sharp(x)=\operatorname{div}(F^\sharp)(x), and (\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{sym}}F)^\sharp(x)=\operatorname{curl}(F^\sharp)(x).

Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → Prop

The equality relation. It has one introduction rule, Eq.refl. We use a = b as notation for Eq a b. A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.

variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd

Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value. That is, given h1 : a = b and h2 : p a, we can construct a proof for p b using substitution: Eq.subst h1 h2. Example:

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2

The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of Eq.subst and Eq.symm, and you can enter it by typing \t. For more information: Equality

Reduced viscous equations on an open profile domain D give the Cartesian vorticity equation at every spacetime point whose (t, s, z) image lies in D. Axis points are covered exactly when D contains a neighbourhood of s = 0, so the profiles must be smooth for slightly negative squared radius as well; this is the even-in-r condition of classical axisymmetric flow. The stream equation identifying this vorticity with curl is a separate condition. Setting viscosity to zero gives the Euler transport equation.

Fact (p : Prop) : Prop

Wrapper for adding elementary propositions to the type class systems. Warning: this can easily be abused. See the rest of this docstring for details.

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally, but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system in specific circumstances.

For example, ZMod p is a field if and only if p is a prime number. In order to be able to find this field instance automatically by type class search, we have to turn p.Prime into an instance implicit assumption.

On the other hand, making Nat.Prime a class would require a major refactoring of the library, and it is questionable whether making Nat.Prime a class is desirable at all. The compromise is to add the assumption [Fact p.Prime] to ZMod.instField.

In particular, this class is not intended for turning the type class system into an automated theorem prover for first-order logic.

Construct a trapezoidal certificate under one total error tolerance.

The backend interval I encloses the exact-real trapezoidal value on the mesh planned with analytic budget tolerance - radius I. Replacing that value by the interval midpoint spends radius I on numerical roundoff. Thus the certificate records the sum of the planned analytic error and the verified roundoff error.

The construction itself does not require the remaining budget to be positive. That condition appears only in the theorem asserting that the requested total tolerance is met.

List.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u

Linked lists: ordered lists, in which each element has a reference to the next element.

Most operations on linked lists take time proportional to the length of the list, because each element must be traversed to find the next element.

List α is isomorphic to Array α, but they are useful for different things:

  • List α is easier for reasoning, and Array α is modeled as a wrapper around List α.
  • List α works well as a persistent data structure, when many copies of the tail are shared. When the value is not shared, Array α will have better performance because it can do destructive updates.

Pointwise Hermite remainder for a derivative chain F on [a, b] and n distinct nodes there. At every x ∈ [a, b] some ξ ∈ [a, b] satisfies F 0 x - H x = F (2n) ξ / (2n)! * P x ^ 2, with H the Hermite interpolant of F 0, F 1 at the nodes and P the nodal polynomial. At a node both sides vanish. Otherwise G = F 0 - H - c P ^ 2 with c = (F 0 x - H x) / P x ^ 2 has double zeros at the nodes and a zero at x, so exists_derivative_chain_zero_of_double_zeros gives ξ with G^(2n) ξ = 0, and H^(2n) = 0, (P ^ 2)^(2n) = (2n)! unwind this to the claim.

Subtype.{u} {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)

All the elements of a type that satisfy a predicate.

Subtype p, usually written { x : α // p x } or { x // p x }, contains all elements x : α for which p x is true. Its constructor is a pair of the value and the proof that it satisfies the predicate. In run-time code, { x : α // p x } is represented identically to α.

There is a coercion from { x : α // p x } to α, so elements of a subtype may be used where the underlying type is expected.

Examples:

  • { n : Nat // n % 2 = 0 } is the type of even numbers.
  • { xs : Array String // xs.size = 5 } is the type of arrays with five Strings.
  • Given xs : List α, List { x : α // x ∈ xs } is the type of lists in which all elements are contained in xs.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

  • The recommended spelling of { x // p x } in identifiers is subtype.

CAS.Tactic.Certificate.closeFromLocalCertificates : Lean.Elab.Tactic.TacticM Unit

Close the main goal from a matching checked certificate in the local context or among the subterms of the target.

Exact projections are tried first. Approximation, residual, bound, model, and quadrature certificates may then be weakened to a larger requested budget; enclosures may be widened at both endpoints. Every generated inequality must be discharged by the shared arithmetic phase. A certificate whose domain differs from the goal's is then restricted to the goal's domain (inferSubsetProof) and tried again in the same way.

This type is special-cased by the compiler and overridden with an efficient implementation. Executable algebraic normalizer for symbolic expressions. It normalizes the operands first. Sums, differences and products go through normalizeAdd, normalizeSub and normalizeMul. The negation of a quotient negates the numerator, and any other negation is polynomial-normalized. A division is rebuilt by mkDiv from its normalized parts, a natural power is polynomial-normalized, and the elementary functions are rebuilt around their normalized arguments. Literals, π, e and variables are returned unchanged. No side condition is recorded: eval_normalize holds at every valuation.

CAS.Verified.Expr.ValidAt.{u_1} {ι : Type u_1} (ρ : ι → ℝ) : CAS.Verified.Expr ι → Prop

Side conditions needed to justify the classical analytic derivative rules.

Rational literals carry a natural-number denominator in the AST, so validity rules out den = 0 there just as it rules out zero denominators for expression-level division.

For log, validity excludes zero, matching Mathlib's derivative theorem for the total real logarithm on both connected components of ℝ \ {0}. For sqrt, validity requires a strictly positive argument. This is stronger than what Mathlib's Real.hasDerivAt_sqrt needs (x ≠ 0, since Real.sqrt is constant on (-∞, 0]): it certifies the classical square-root branch rather than the totalized function, so a goal that is Lean-true only because of the extension to negative arguments is rejected by the reflective route. Lean's total Real.log/Real.sqrt have values outside those analytic domains, but these symbolic derivative rules certify classical differentiability. Raw Expr.eval itself is total and does not require ValidAt.

For rpow a b, validity requires a strictly positive base 0 < a, the hypothesis of Mathlib's HasFDerivAt.rpow; Lean's total Real.rpow has values for nonpositive bases that the classical power rule does not certify.

For asin and acos, validity excludes the two endpoints -1 and 1, matching Mathlib's derivative theorems for the total real inverse trigonometric functions. Arguments outside [-1, 1] are allowed: there the functions are locally constant and their derivatives are zero. Unlike sqrt and rpow, these cases do not restrict evaluation to the classical branch.

ContDiffAt.{u, uE, uF} (𝕜 : Type u) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type uE} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (n : WithTop ℕ∞) (f : E → F) (x : E) : Prop

A function is continuously differentiable up to n at a point x if, for any integer k ≤ n, there is a neighborhood of x where f admits derivatives up to order n, which are continuous. The parameter n belongs to ℕ∞ω (accessible in the ContDiff scope), i.e. it can be a natural number, ∞, or ω.

For n = ∞, we only require that this holds up to any finite order (where the neighborhood may depend on the finite order we consider). For n = ω, we require the function to be analytic at x. The precise definition we give (all the derivatives should be analytic) is more involved to work around issues when the space is not complete, but it is equivalent when the space is complete.

The FloatLib expression with the value of expr, where variable i is the input at index vars i (eval_toFloatLib). A box with coordinates Fin n takes vars := Fin.val, and labels of any other type are numbered by occurrence first (numberOccurrences).

Literals become rational constants, and π, a ^ b and e are the calls 0, 1 and 2 of FloatLib's standard calls Backend.Standard.extensions. Evaluate an expression as Expr.eval? does, with one more rule: a product with a factor that is exactly zero, and a quotient with such a numerator, have the enclosure of that zero whether or not the other operand has an enclosure (Expr.zeroOperand?). So 0 * (1 / x) has the enclosure of zero on a box that contains x = 0, where Expr.eval? has none. Every enclosure of Expr.eval? is the enclosure here (Expr.evalZero?_of_eval?).

The definition is the recursor of Expr, as that of Expr.eval? is. Expr.evalZero?_const to Expr.evalZero?_call state the recursion by pattern matching, and compiled code runs Expr.Compiled.evalZero? (Expr.evalZero?_eq_compiled).

The disjoint union of types α and β, ordinarily written α ⊕ β.

An element of α ⊕ β is either an a : α wrapped in Sum.inl or a b : β wrapped in Sum.inr. α ⊕ β is not equivalent to the set-theoretic union of α and β because its values include an indication of which of the two types was chosen. The implementation is reducible to Mathlib's MvPowerSeries, so all algebraic laws and coefficient convolution theorems are inherited rather than reproved. Extraction and composition take that index as an explicit policy, not as a typing invariant. id.{u} {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α

The identity function. id takes an implicit argument α : Sort u (a type in any universe), and an argument a : α, and returns a.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If e has type T, and T' is definitionally equal to T, then @id T' e typechecks, and Lean knows that this expression has type T' rather than T. HasSum.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [AddCommMonoid α] [TopologicalSpace α] (f : β → α) (a : α) (L : SummationFilter β := SummationFilter.unconditional β) : Prop

HasSum f a L means that the (potentially infinite) sum of the f b for b : β converges to a along the SummationFilter L.

By default L is the unconditional one, corresponding to the limit of all finite sets towards the entire type. So we take the sum over bigger and bigger finite sets. This sum operation is invariant under permuting the terms (while sums for more general summation filters usually are not). This is based on Mario Carneiro's infinite sum df-tsms in Metamath.

In particular, the function ℕ → ℝ sending n to (-1) ^ n / (n + 1) does not have a sum for this definition, although it is summable for the conditional summation filter that takes limits of sums over n ∈ {0, ..., X} as X → ∞. However, a series which is absolutely convergent with respect to the conditional summation filter is in fact unconditionally summable.

For the definition and many statements, α does not need to be a topological additive monoid, only an additive monoid with a topology (i.e. the addition is not assumed to be continuous). We only add this assumption later, for the lemmas where it is relevant.

The heat-kernel evolution preserves uniform bounds.

If the continuous initial datum satisfies |g| ≤ M, then its heat evolution satisfies the same pointwise bound at every time; taking the optimal M, this is the L∞ contraction property of the heat semigroup. For t ≤ 0 this is the bound on g itself. For t > 0, positivity of the Gaussian kernel, its unit mass, and the Bochner integral triangle inequality give

|Γ_t * g| ≤ Γ_t * |g| ≤ M Γ_t * 1 = M.

Evans obtains the same bound for solutions with the growth bound (24) from his §2.3.3(a), Theorem 6 (Maximum principle for the Cauchy problem), applied to u and -u. Continuity of g is used only for measurability.

The Banach space of bounded γ-Hölder real-valued functions on a metric type Ω, equipped with ‖f‖∞ + [f]γ.

For a geometric domain, take Ω to be the corresponding subtype.

MetricSpace.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u

A metric space is a type endowed with a ℝ-valued distance dist satisfying dist x y = 0 ↔ x = y, commutativity dist x y = dist y x, and the triangle inequality dist x z ≤ dist x y + dist y z.

See pseudometric spaces (PseudoMetricSpace) for the similar class with the dist x y = 0 ↔ x = y assumption weakened to dist x x = 0.

Any metric space is a T1 topological space and a uniform space (see TopologicalSpace, T1Space, UniformSpace), where the topology and uniformity come from the metric.

We make the uniformity/topology part of the data instead of deriving it from the metric. This e.g. ensures that we do not get a diamond when doing [MetricSpace α] [MetricSpace β] : TopologicalSpace (α × β): The product metric and product topology agree, but not definitionally so. See Note [forgetful inheritance].

PseudoEMetricSpace.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u

A pseudo extended metric space is a type endowed with a ℝ≥0∞-valued distance edist satisfying reflexivity edist x x = 0, commutativity edist x y = edist y x, and the triangle inequality edist x z ≤ edist x y + edist y z.

Note that we do not require edist x y = 0 → x = y. See extended metric spaces (EMetricSpace) for the similar class with that stronger assumption.

Any pseudo extended metric space is a topological space and a uniform space (see TopologicalSpace, UniformSpace), where the topology and uniformity come from the metric. Note that a T1 pseudo extended metric space is just an extended metric space.

We make the uniformity/topology part of the data instead of deriving it from the metric. This e.g. ensures that we do not get a diamond when doing [PseudoEMetricSpace α] [PseudoEMetricSpace β] : TopologicalSpace (α × β): The product metric and product topology agree, but not definitionally so. See Note [forgetful inheritance].

The recursive derivative data underlying an order-m Sobolev time jet.

At order zero there is only an L²_t L²_x trajectory. At successor order, the head is H^{m+1}-valued, its weak time derivative is an H^m-valued trajectory, and that derivative itself carries the remaining order-m jet. The canonical map H^{m+1} → H^m is inserted before stating the weak derivative identity in the identity Gelfand triple on H^m.

This is an ordinary Hilbert-valued weak derivative, not an additional PDE assumption. The Gelfand form is used because the Lions-Magenes theorem then supplies the canonical representative continuous through both time endpoints.

This recursive shape avoids storing the same analytic object at unrelated dependent indices. It makes the induction in Evans literal: differentiating once means taking the recursive tail.

u_tt(t) + B(t)u(t) = ell(t)

The explicit two-step level recurrence behind the nonsymmetric version of Evans estimate (64).

Level zero is the highest time derivative in L²; level one is the next derivative in H¹. For k ≥ 0 the majorant is defined by

C_{k+2} = S_k (F_k + C_k + |μ| E_k C_{k+1}).

Here S_k plays the role of the norm of the shifted H^k → H^{k+2} solver, F_k of the pointwise forcing factor, and E_k of the norm of the restriction from H^{k+1} to H^k. solutionSobolevNormSum_le_of_nonsymmetricSpatialRecurrence takes the recurrence with these constants as a hypothesis.

The principal part A is symmetric and coercive on the energy space, while R is allowed to be nonsymmetric and is controlled in the mixed V x H norm. Stable dense trial projections, compatible ambient initial data, a coherent forcing chain, and the uniform forcing budget generate a finite chain of ambient weak-wave solutions for the full operator A + R, provided hRitz holds:

(A + R) (q r.succ - P_k (q r.succ)) w = 0

for every trial level k, adjacent jet index r, and test w in that trial space. Here P_k is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to V. This full-operator condition is separate from stability and density.

All finite-dimensional trajectories, their uniform bounds, and their common weak limit are constructed in the proof. In particular, no limiting weak wave or higher-regularity conclusion is included among the hypotheses.

At level n, the acceleration is only the residual precomposed with the trial projection:

accelerationₙ = (ell - B(·)uₙ) ∘ Pₙ.

This is the finite-dimensional statement: in general a Galerkin approximation does not solve the ambient equation in all of V*. Assume a bounded projected Galerkin family with the same exact initial displacement q₀ and velocity p₀ at every index. Suppose in addition that estimate (52) has supplied dimension-independent essential bounds

‖uₘ(t)‖_V ≤ Cᵤ and ‖uₘ'(t)‖_H ≤ Cᵥ.

Then the compactness construction produces a weak solution satisfying

u ∈ L∞(a,b;V) and u_t ∈ L∞(a,b;H),

with the same almost-everywhere bounds. In concrete divergence-form wave problems, ae_norm_displacementLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le and ae_norm_velocityLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le supply these two additional hypotheses from the coercive Galerkin energy estimate.

The proof uses the same common ultrafilter for displacement, velocity, and acceleration. The weak-wave equations are passed to the limit exactly as in exists_of_bounded_projected_galerkin_family, while improvedRegularity_of_weak_L2_limits preserves the closed convex essential norm balls. Thus the regularity conclusion is proved rather than stored as extra data in the definition of a weak solution.

Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(ii): identification of the differentiated Galerkin limits.

Suppose one common filter gives weak limits for an original Galerkin family and its differentiated family. The exact finite-dimensional identities

J (duₘ) = velocityₘ,

J* (dvelocityₘ) = accelerationₘ

then survive weak convergence. If the coefficient derivative identity d uₘ/dt = duₘ is also retained in the identity Gelfand triple, the limit du is the V-valued weak derivative of u.

Uniform essential bounds on duₘ in V and dvelocityₘ in H pass to the same limits by weak closedness of the almost-everywhere norm balls. Finally, for an autonomous operator and weakly differentiable forcing, the theorem constructs u_{ttt} in L²(a,b;V*).

This is the compactness/identification step that cannot be justified by extracting unrelated subnets for the original and differentiated systems.

Local weak differentiation in time for functions valued in a real normed space. The definition records local Bochner integrability as well as the standard distributional identity against smooth scalar tests whose topological support lies in U. Including integrability is essential: Lean's Bochner integral is defined to be zero for a nonintegrable function, so the identity alone would not characterize a distributional derivative.

On Set.univ, this is the global weak-time-derivative predicate. On a proper open interval, compactly supported tests vanish near both endpoints, so the relation places no condition on endpoint traces or values outside the interval.

Nothing in the definition is specific to time: it is the weak derivative of any function of one real variable, and the De Gregorio profile files apply it to the spatial variable of a stationary profile.

Weak sequential/net closure of Evans's weak-wave solution predicate.

Suppose a family of weak-wave solutions has a common weak limit in the three natural Bochner spaces:

  • displacement in L²(a,b;V),
  • velocity in L²(a,b;H), and
  • acceleration in L²(a,b;V*).

The acceleration convergence is stated after Riesz transport, matching the Hilbert weak topology used by the compactness theorem. Then the three limit objects again satisfy the weak-wave predicate with the same initial data and forcing.

The proof follows the Evans limit passage:

  1. bounded linearity of H → V* passes the displacement identity;
  2. fixed space-time testing passes the velocity identity; and
  3. bounded operator-valued multiplication passes B(t)u weakly, so uniqueness of weak limits yields u_tt + B(t)u = ell in L²(V*).

We use Mathlib's test-function type 𝓓((⊤ : Opens (ℝ^n)), ℝ) and require its tsupport (closed support) to lie in Ω. When Ω is open, this is the test class C_c^∞(Ω) of Evans §5.2.1.

Both f and its proposed weak derivative g are required to lie in L¹_loc(Ω), and the sign is (-1)^|α|, exactly as in Evans §5.2.1, (3). For an arbitrary set the predicate is still a well-formed test-function relation, but it is not automatically the standard Sobolev weak derivative: the test class can be too small (and can be trivial when Ω has empty interior), so uniqueness may fail. Results identifying this relation with the usual weak derivative therefore require openness or another explicit test-function density hypothesis.

existsUnique_of_measurable_galerkin_garding_L2 constructs the unique Bochner class solving the integrated weak equation. This theorem adds the data that Evans uses to define the parabolic weak solution and its a priori theory:

  • the weak time derivative belongs to L²(a,b;V*);
  • u_t = ell - B(·)u almost everywhere;
  • the state has a representative continuous from [a,b] into the pivot Hilbert space H, with left trace equal to uInit;
  • the representative satisfies the Gårding energy estimate on every prefix [a,t].

Thus the measurable Galerkin construction produces a weak solution in the sense of Evans §7.1.1, with the continuity into H that Evans obtains from §5.9.2, Theorem 3.

A class stating that p q r : ℝ≥0∞ satisfy p⁻¹ + q⁻¹ = r⁻¹. This is exactly the condition for which Hölder's inequality is valid (see MeasureTheory.MemLp.smul).

The rank of a module as a natural number.

For a finite-dimensional vector space V over a field k, Module.finrank k V is equal to the dimension of V over k.

For a general module M over a ring R, Module.finrank R M is defined to be the supremum of the cardinalities of the R-linearly independent subsets of M, if this supremum is finite. It is defined by convention to be 0 if this supremum is infinite. See Module.rank for a cardinal-valued version where infinite rank modules have rank an infinite cardinal.

Note that if R is not a field then there can exist modules M with ¬(Module.Finite R M) but finrank R M ≠ 0. For example ℚ has finrank equal to 1 over ℤ, because the nonempty ℤ-linearly independent subsets of ℚ are precisely the nonzero singletons.

u is a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u) on Ω: on every open V with compact closure in Ω, every W^{1,2}(V) element that represents u has no more energy than its perturbation by any smooth function with compact support in V.

The perturbations may be large, and they are the smallest class in use, so among the notions that compare with all perturbations in a class this is the weakest. Nothing is asked of u outside such sets V, and Ω need not be bounded.

The predicate does not say that u is in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω): on a set V where u has no representative in W^{1,2}(V) it asks nothing. It does not say that the energies are finite either: the integrals are Bochner integrals, which are 0 for a density that is not integrable. The regularity theorems assume IsLocallyWkpOn 1 2 Ω u and a density with Lipschitz gradient, for which every energy is finite (integrable_gradientDensity_of_lipschitzWith).

Solutions of the Lagrangian equation are analytic. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be open and let F be a uniformly regular integrand. Every function v with two continuous derivatives on Ω that satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation div(∇F(∇v)) = 0 at every point of Ω is real-analytic on Ω. In Hilbert's words, the equation admits "analytic integrals exclusively" among the functions of class C².

This is PDE.CalculusOfVariations.analyticOnNhd_of_contDiffOn_two: a classical solution is a local minimizer, because F is convex.

A uniformly regular integrand F(∇z) of one unknown function of n variables: F is real-analytic, and its second derivative satisfies θ |ξ|² ≤ D²F(p)(ξ, ξ) ≤ Λ |ξ|² for all p and ξ, with θ > 0. For two variables this implies Hilbert's inequality F_pp F_qq - F_pq² > 0 (IsRegular.hilbert_inequality).

Hilbert's nineteenth problem for one unknown. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be open and let F be a uniformly regular integrand. Every local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u) in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω) has a representative that is real-analytic on Ω and satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation div(∇F(∇v)) = 0 at every point of Ω.

Hilbert's inequality. For two variables, a uniformly regular integrand satisfies F_pp > 0 and F_pp F_qq - F_pq² > 0 at every point, where F_pp, F_pq and F_qq are the second derivatives of F in the two coordinate directions. So it defines a regular variation problem in Hilbert's sense, with a positive definite second derivative.

With a = F_pp, c = F_qq, d = F_pq the lower bound says that (a - θ) s² + 2 d s t + (c - θ) t² ≥ 0 for all s, t. Hence d² ≤ (a - θ)(c - θ), and a c - d² ≥ θ (a + c) - θ² ≥ θ².

A solution with given boundary values is analytic inside. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be bounded and open and let F be a uniformly regular integrand. If u solves the variational problem of the twentieth problem for the integrand F(∇z) of one unknown, with the boundary values of any g ∈ W^{1,2}(Ω), then u has a representative that is real-analytic on Ω and satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation at every point of Ω. The datum need not be continuous or analytic.

A minimizer in the boundary class is a local minimizer (isLocalMinimizerOn_of_prescribed_boundary), and IsRegular.exists_analytic applies.

u solves the variational problem with boundary values g: it has these boundary values, its integral is finite, and no system with these boundary values and a finite integral has a smaller one. "Finite" means that F(x, u, Du) is integrable. For an integrand that is bounded below by an integrable function, a system on which F(x, v, Dv) is not integrable has integral +∞, so this is minimality among all systems with the boundary values.

The nineteenth and the twentieth problem together. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be bounded and open, n ≥ 1, and let F be a uniformly regular integrand. For every boundary datum g ∈ W^{1,2}(Ω) the variational problem for ∫ F(∇z) has a solution with the boundary values of g, in the sense u - g ∈ W₀^{1,2}(Ω), and the solution has a representative that is real-analytic in Ω.

Then the first variation of the integral at u vanishes in every direction with zero boundary values. No convexity is assumed.

Dirichlet's principle. On a bounded measurable set of positive dimension, for every number of unknowns, every 1 < p < ∞ and every boundary datum g ∈ W^{1,p}, the integral ∫ |Du|ᵖ has a minimizer u with the boundary values of g, and ∫ p |Du|^{p-2} ⟪Du, Dφ⟫ = 0 for every φ with zero boundary values. For p = 2 the integral is Dirichlet's and u is weakly harmonic. Every premise of exists_isWeakSolution holds here.

Hilbert's twentieth problem for the Euler–Lagrange system. On a bounded measurable set of positive dimension, for 1 < p < ∞, a convex integrand of growth p with a derivative of growth p - 1 and every boundary datum g ∈ W^{1,p}, there is a system u with the boundary values of g that is a weak solution of the Euler–Lagrange system. It is a solution of the variational problem.

PDE.HilbertProblems.Twentieth.IsConvexIntegrand {m n : ℕ} (Ω : Set ℝ^n) (p : NNReal) (F : ℝ^n → ℝ^m × ℝ^(m * n) → ℝ) : Prop

A convex integrand of growth p on Ω: F(x, s, ξ) is jointly measurable and, for almost every x in Ω, continuous in the value s, convex in the derivatives ξ, at least c |ξ|ᵖ - b(x) with c > 0 and b integrable, and at most a(x) + D |(s, ξ)|ᵖ with a integrable. The norm of the pair (s, ξ) is the larger of the two Euclidean norms. Convexity in ξ is what existence uses of a positive definite second derivative, Hilbert's regularity. The two bounds keep a minimizing sequence bounded and the integral finite.

Hilbert's twentieth problem, existence. On a bounded measurable set of positive dimension, for 1 < p < ∞, every variational problem with a convex integrand of growth p has a solution for every boundary datum g ∈ W^{1,p}: a system u with the boundary values of g whose integral ∫ F(x, u, Du) is finite and least among all systems with these boundary values. The number of unknown functions is arbitrary, the integrand need not be differentiable and the boundary of the set need not be regular.

This is the direct method, with lower semicontinuity from convexity in the derivatives: exists_minimizer_integral_vectorWkp_prescribed_boundary.

The Sobolev system of boundary data g that are continuously differentiable up to the boundary of a bounded open set: each g i is continuously differentiable in Ω, and it and its first derivatives are uniformly continuous there, so they extend continuously to the closure. Such a system lies in W^{1,p} for every p. It depends only on the values of g inside Ω; the boundary values meant are those of the continuous extension.

Hilbert's independence theorem for a multiple integral, for a family of extremal surfaces. Let Ω be a bounded open set with C¹ graph boundary, and let z = Z t, t ∈ J, be solutions of the Euler–Lagrange system of ∫ F(Dz, z; x) dx on Ω (IsExtremalFamily). Let θ and θ' be C¹ functions with values in J (IsGraphParameter) that agree on the boundary of Ω; then the surfaces z(x) = Z (θ x) x and z'(x) = Z (θ' x) x pass through the same boundary curve. The integral J* = ∫ {F(P) + (Dz - P) F_P(P)} dω has the same value along the two surfaces. Both integrands are integrable (integrableOn_fieldIntegrand).

This is ExtremalFamily.integral_invariant_eq_of_eqOn_frontier, through integral_fieldIntegrand.

Independence of the surface through a given boundary curve. Under the hypotheses of multipleIntegral_independence on the family, suppose that over every boundary point the surfaces of the family do not meet: t ↦ Z t x is injective on J. If the surfaces z(x) = Z (θ x) x and z'(x) = Z (θ' x) x have the same boundary values, J* has the same value along both. This is Hilbert's statement, "independent of the choice of the surface passing through the given closed twisted curve", for the parameter graphs of the family.

Equal boundary values and injectivity give equal parameters on the boundary. Without injectivity the conclusion can fail.

A function is continuously differentiable up to order n within a set s at a point x if it admits continuous derivatives up to order n in a neighborhood of x in s ∪ {x}. Replaces a value with its difference from the largest value in the type.

Considering the values of Fin n as a sequence 0, 1, …, n-2, n-1, Fin.rev finds the corresponding element of the reversed sequence. In other words, it maps 0 to n-1, 1 to n-2, ..., and n-1 to 0.
