PDE.contDiff_partialDeriv_timeTrace.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {m : ℕ} (i : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → E) (x : ℝ^n) (hf : ContDiff ℝ (↑m + 1) f) : ContDiff ℝ ↑m fun t ↦ (∂[i] fun y ↦ f (y, t)) x

A spatial derivative evaluated at a fixed point inherits one fewer derivative as a function of time.

PDE.contDiff_secondPartialDeriv_timeTrace.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {m : ℕ} (i j : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → E) (x : ℝ^n) (hf : ContDiff ℝ (↑m + 2) f) : ContDiff ℝ ↑m fun t ↦ (∂[i] fun y ↦ (∂[j] fun z ↦ f (z, t)) y) x

Two spatial derivatives evaluated at a fixed point inherit two fewer derivatives as a function of time.
ContDiff ℝ (↑m + 2) f

PDE.deriv_partialDeriv_timeSlice_comm.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → E) (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) (hf : ContDiff ℝ 2 f) : deriv (fun s ↦ (∂[i] fun y ↦ f (y, s)) x) t = (∂[i] fun y ↦ deriv (fun s ↦ f (y, s)) t) x

For a globally C² spacetime field, one spatial derivative commutes with differentiation of a fixed-space time trace.

PDE.deriv_prod_timeSlice.{u_1, u_2} {D : Type u_1} {E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup D] [NormedSpace ℝ D] [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (f : D × ℝ → E) (x : D) (t : ℝ) (hf : DifferentiableAt ℝ f (x, t)) : deriv (fun s ↦ f (x, s)) t = (fderiv ℝ f (x, t)) (0, 1)

A scalar-parameter slice has the joint derivative in direction (0, 1).
DifferentiableAt ℝ f (x, t)

PDE.deriv_secondPartialDeriv_timeSlice_comm.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i j : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → E) (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) (hf : ContDiff ℝ 3 f) : deriv (fun s ↦ (∂[i] fun y ↦ (∂[j] fun z ↦ f (z, s)) y) x) t = (∂[i] fun y ↦ (∂[j] fun z ↦ deriv (fun s ↦ f (z, s)) t) y) x

For a globally C³ spacetime field, two spatial derivatives commute with differentiation of a fixed-space time trace.
ContDiff ℝ 3 f

PDE.differentiableAt_time_slice_of_contDiffOn.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {I : Set ℝ} (hI : IsOpen I) (u : ℝ^n × ℝ → E) (hu : ContDiffOn ℝ 1 u (Set.univ ×ˢ I)) (x : ℝ^n) {t : ℝ} (ht : t ∈ I) : DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun s ↦ u (x, s)) t

Joint C¹ regularity on an open spacetime cylinder implies differentiability of every fixed-space time curve.

So classical solution predicates need not assume time differentiability separately: it follows from joint spacetime regularity.
IsOpen I
ContDiffOn ℝ 1 u (Set.univ ×ˢ I)
t ∈ I

PDE.divergence {n : ℕ} (F : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) (x : ℝ^n) : ℝ

Divergence of a vector field, ∑ᵢ ∂ᵢ Fᵢ.

Each scalar component is differentiated using the total fderiv expression. Differentiability of the components at x gives the classical divergence there. The trace formula for the derivative of the whole field requires differentiability of F; without that hypothesis, these two total expressions need not agree.

PDE.fderiv_apply_eq_sum_partialDeriv_mul {n : ℕ} (f : ℝ^n → ℝ) (x v : ℝ^n) : (fderiv ℝ f x) v = ∑ j, ∂[j] f x * v.ofLp j

Scalar specialization of fderiv_apply_eq_sum_smul_partialDeriv.

PDE.fderiv_apply_eq_sum_smul_partialDeriv.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (f : ℝ^n → E) (x v : ℝ^n) : (fderiv ℝ f x) v = ∑ j, v.ofLp j • ∂[j] f x

Expand a Fréchet derivative in the Euclidean coordinate basis.

The codomain is an arbitrary real normed space, so the same formula covers scalar advection and vector-valued transport.

PDE.fderiv_joinSpaceTime_spatial.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (u : PDE.SpaceTime n → E) (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) (hu : DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) : (fderiv ℝ (fun p ↦ u (PDE.Common.joinSpaceTime p)) (x, t)) (EuclideanSpace.single i 1, 0) = ∂[i.succ] u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)

A spatial direction of the (x,t) product pullback is coordinate i+1 in canonical Euclidean spacetime.
DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)

PDE.fderiv_joinSpaceTime_time.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (u : PDE.SpaceTime n → E) (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) (hu : DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) : (fderiv ℝ (fun p ↦ u (PDE.Common.joinSpaceTime p)) (x, t)) (0, 1) = ∂[0] u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)

The time direction of the (x,t) product pullback is coordinate zero in canonical Euclidean spacetime.

PDE.fderiv_timeSpaceCons_time.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (u : ℝ^(n + 1) → E) (t : ℝ) (x : ℝ^n) (hu : DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) : (fderiv ℝ (fun p ↦ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons p.1 p.2)) (t, x)) (1, 0) = ∂[0] u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)

Applying the derivative of a spacetime pullback in the time direction recovers the zeroth coordinate derivative of the original field.

PDE.gradient_apply_eq_partialDeriv {n : ℕ} (f : ℝ^n → ℝ) (x : ℝ^n) (i : Fin n) : (gradient f x).ofLp i = ∂[i] f x

The ith coordinate of Mathlib's gradient is PDEAtlas's ith partial derivative.

Both sides are total expressions built from fderiv. Reading them as classical derivatives requires the usual differentiability hypothesis.

PDE.hasDerivAt_timeSpaceCons.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (u : ℝ^(n + 1) → E) (t : ℝ) (x : ℝ^n) (hu : DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) : HasDerivAt (fun s ↦ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons s x)) (∂[0] u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) t

The derivative along a fixed spatial point is the time-coordinate derivative of the spacetime field.

PDE.iterate_partialDeriv_comm.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : ℝ^n → E} (i j : Fin n) (a b : ℕ) (hf : ContDiff ℝ (↑a + ↑b) f) : (fun g x ↦ ∂[i] g x)^[a] ((fun g x ↦ ∂[j] g x)^[b] f) = (fun g x ↦ ∂[j] g x)^[b] ((fun g x ↦ ∂[i] g x)^[a] f)

Coordinate blocks of lengths a and b commute for a C^(a+b) function. This is the block form needed when a PDE operator is differentiated by a mixed multi-index.
ContDiff ℝ (↑a + ↑b) f

PDE.iterate_partialDeriv_congr_nhds.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (m : ℕ) {f g : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} (h : f =ᶠ[nhds x] g) : (fun q y ↦ ∂[i] q y)^[m] f x = (fun q y ↦ ∂[i] q y)^[m] g x

Repeated coordinate partials at a point depend only on the germ of the function there.

PDE.iterate_partialDeriv_eq_iteratedFDeriv_single.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (m : ℕ) {f : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} (hf : ContDiffAt ℝ (↑m) f x) : (fun g y ↦ ∂[i] g y)^[m] f x = (iteratedFDeriv ℝ m f x) fun x ↦ EuclideanSpace.single i 1

Repeating one coordinate partial m times is the m-th Fréchet derivative evaluated on m copies of the corresponding coordinate unit vector. Unlike the block-commutation results below, this pointwise theorem needs only local C^m regularity at the evaluation point.
ContDiffAt ℝ (↑m) f x

PDE.iterate_partialDeriv_eventuallyEq.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (m : ℕ) {f g : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} (h : f =ᶠ[nhds x] g) : (fun q y ↦ ∂[i] q y)^[m] f =ᶠ[nhds x] (fun q y ↦ ∂[i] q y)^[m] g

Germ equality propagates to a repeated coordinate derivative. No regularity is needed, since the coordinate derivatives are those of the total derivative.

PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv_add_of_contDiff.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f g : ℝ^n → E} (indices : List (Fin n)) (hf : ContDiff ℝ (↑indices.length) f) (hg : ContDiff ℝ (↑indices.length) g) : (fun x ↦ PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices (f + g) x) = fun x ↦ PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices f x + PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices g x

Iterated coordinate derivatives distribute over addition under the minimal finite regularity hypothesis.
ContDiff ℝ (↑indices.length) f
ContDiff ℝ (↑indices.length) g

PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv_append_single.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (indices : List (Fin n)) (i : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n → E) (x : ℝ^n) : PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv (indices ++ [i]) f x = PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices (fun y ↦ ∂[i] f y) x

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

  • The recommended spelling of ++ in identifiers is append.

PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv_const_smul.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (c : ℝ) (indices : List (Fin n)) (f : ℝ^n → E) : (fun x ↦ PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices (c • f) x) = fun x ↦ c • PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices f x

PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv_sub_of_contDiff.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f g : ℝ^n → E} (indices : List (Fin n)) (hf : ContDiff ℝ (↑indices.length) f) (hg : ContDiff ℝ (↑indices.length) g) : (fun x ↦ PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices (f - g) x) = fun x ↦ PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices f x - PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices g x

Iterated coordinate derivatives distribute over subtraction under the minimal finite regularity hypothesis.

PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv_zero.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (indices : List (Fin n)) (x : ℝ^n) : PDE.iteratedPartialDeriv indices 0 x = 0

Every iterated coordinate derivative of the zero function vanishes.

PDE.laplaceEquation (n : ℕ) : PDE.LinearPDE ℝ (ℝ^n) ℝ 2

The Laplace equation Δu = 0 in dimension n.

For n = 0, the coordinate sum is empty and the operator is identically zero. Analytic PDE applications should assume 0 < n.

PDE.laplaceEquation_residual (n : ℕ) (u : ℝ^n → ℝ) (x : ℝ^n) : (PDE.laplaceEquation n).residual u x = PDE.laplacian u x

The identity holds for every u; reading it as the classical Laplacian requires u ∈ C².

No regularity or domain condition is built in. Reading this value as a classical PDE residual needs the C^k hypothesis on u and x ∈ pde.domain.

ℝ^n ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] ℝ^n
ContDiffAt ℝ 2 f (A x + b)

The coordinate Laplacian is invariant under a linear isometry at a C² point.
ContDiffAt ℝ 2 f (A x)

The coordinate Laplacian is the divergence of Mathlib's gradient.

ContDiffAt ℝ 2 f x
ContDiffAt ℝ 2 g x

PDE.mixed_iterate_partialDeriv_congr_nhds.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i j : Fin n) (a b : ℕ) {f g : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} (h : f =ᶠ[nhds x] g) : (fun q y ↦ ∂[i] q y)^[a] ((fun q y ↦ ∂[j] q y)^[b] f) x = (fun q y ↦ ∂[i] q y)^[a] ((fun q y ↦ ∂[j] q y)^[b] g) x

Nested blocks of two coordinate derivatives at a point depend only on the germ of the function there.

PDE.partialDeriv.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n → E) (x : ℝ^n) : E

Partial derivative expression ∂ᵢ f(x) for a Euclidean-domain map.

This is total because it is defined using Mathlib's fderiv; it does not itself assert that f is differentiable at x.

PDE.partialDeriv_add.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {i : Fin n} {f g : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} (hf : DifferentiableAt ℝ f x) (hg : DifferentiableAt ℝ g x) : (∂[i] fun y ↦ f y + g y) x = ∂[i] f x + ∂[i] g x

Partial derivative of a sum is the sum of partial derivatives.
DifferentiableAt ℝ f x
DifferentiableAt ℝ g x

PDE.partialDeriv_const_smul.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (c : ℝ) {i : Fin n} {f : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} : (∂[i] fun y ↦ c • f y) x = c • ∂[i] f x

A constant scalar can be pulled through a partial derivative.

Unlike the sum rule, this identity needs no differentiability hypothesis: Mathlib's total Fréchet derivative commutes with scalar multiplication even at points where the derivative is defined to be zero.

PDE.partialDeriv_eq_deriv_coordinateLine.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : ℝ^n → E} (i : Fin n) (x : ℝ^n) (hf : DifferentiableAt ℝ f x) : ∂[i] f x = deriv (f ∘ PDE.coordinateLine i x) (x.ofLp i)

At a point of differentiability, a coordinate partial derivative is the ordinary derivative of the restriction to the corresponding coordinate line.

PDE.coordinateLine {n : ℕ} (i : Fin n) (x : ℝ^n) (s : ℝ) : ℝ^n

The affine line through x obtained by varying only coordinate i.

PDE.partialDeriv_iterate_partialDeriv_comm.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : ℝ^n → E} (i j : Fin n) (m : ℕ) (hf : ContDiff ℝ (↑m + 1) f) : (fun g x ↦ ∂[i] g x) ((fun g x ↦ ∂[j] g x)^[m] f) = (fun g x ↦ ∂[j] g x)^[m] fun x ↦ ∂[i] f x

One coordinate derivative commutes with a block of m derivatives in another coordinate for a C^(m+1) function.

PDE.partialDeriv_neg.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {i : Fin n} {f : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} : ∂[i] (-f) x = -∂[i] f x

Partial derivative of a negation is the negation of the partial derivative.

PDE.partialDeriv_partialDeriv_comm_at.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : ℝ^n → E} (i j : Fin n) {x : ℝ^n} (hf : ContDiffAt ℝ 2 f x) : (∂[i] fun y ↦ ∂[j] f y) x = (∂[j] fun y ↦ ∂[i] f y) x

Pointwise Clairaut theorem for Euclidean coordinate partials. A C² germ at x is enough; the proof uses Mathlib's symmetry theorem for the second Fréchet derivative.

PDE.partialDeriv_partialDeriv_comm_of_contDiff.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : ℝ^n → E} (i j : Fin n) (hf : ContDiff ℝ 2 f) : (fun x ↦ (∂[i] fun y ↦ ∂[j] f y) x) = fun x ↦ (∂[j] fun y ↦ ∂[i] f y) x

Function-valued form of coordinate commutation for a C² function.

PDE.partialDeriv_prod_spaceSlice.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → E) (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) (hf : DifferentiableAt ℝ f (x, t)) : (∂[i] fun y ↦ f (y, t)) x = (fderiv ℝ f (x, t)) (EuclideanSpace.single i 1, 0)

A coordinate derivative of a fixed-time spatial slice is the derivative of the joint spacetime field in the corresponding spatial direction.

PDE.partialDeriv_sub.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {i : Fin n} {f g : ℝ^n → E} {x : ℝ^n} (hf : DifferentiableAt ℝ f x) (hg : DifferentiableAt ℝ g x) : (∂[i] fun y ↦ f y - g y) x = ∂[i] f x - ∂[i] g x

Partial derivative of a difference is the difference of partial derivatives.

PDE.partialDeriv_timeSpaceCons_eq_deriv.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (u : ℝ^(n + 1) → E) (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) (hu : DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) : ∂[0] u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x) = deriv (fun s ↦ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons s x)) t

The time-coordinate partial derivative is the derivative of the fixed-space time curve.

PDE.partialDeriv_timeSpaceCons_spatial.{u_1} {n : ℕ} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (i : Fin n) (u : ℝ^(n + 1) → E) (t : ℝ) (x : ℝ^n) (hu : DifferentiableAt ℝ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)) : (∂[i] fun y ↦ u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t y)) x = ∂[i.succ] u (PDE.Common.timeSpaceCons t x)

A spatial coordinate derivative of a fixed-time slice is the corresponding spacetime coordinate derivative.

Interior equations.

PDE.PDEEquation.rhs.{uE, uF, uG} {E : Type uE} {F : Type uF} (self : PDE.PDEEquation E F) : E → self.Output

Right-hand side.

PDE.PDEEquation.domain.{uE, uF, uG} {E : Type uE} {F : Type uF} (self : PDE.PDEEquation E F) : Set E

Set on which the equation is imposed.

PDE.PDEProblem.sideConditions.{uE, uF, uG} {E : Type uE} {F : Type uF} (self : PDE.PDEProblem E F) : List (PDE.PDEEquation E F)

Initial, boundary, normalization, or other designated side equations.

PDE.secondPartialDeriv_mul {n : ℕ} (i j : Fin n) {f g : ℝ^n → ℝ} {x : ℝ^n} (hf : ContDiffAt ℝ 2 f x) (hg : ContDiffAt ℝ 2 g x) : (∂[i] fun y ↦ (∂[j] fun z ↦ f z * g z) y) x = (∂[i] fun y ↦ ∂[j] f y) x * g x + ∂[j] f x * ∂[i] g x + ∂[i] f x * ∂[j] g x + f x * (∂[i] fun y ↦ ∂[j] g y) x

The second mixed coordinate derivative of a product at a C² point.

PDE.spatialGradient_apply {n : ℕ} (u : ℝ^(n + 1) → ℝ) (x : ℝ^(n + 1)) (i : Fin n) : (PDE.spatialGradient u x).ofLp i = ∂[i.succ] u x

The ith spatial-gradient component is spacetime coordinate derivative i.succ; the time coordinate 0 does not appear.

A representative-level package of Lᵖ functions and weak-derivative witnesses on Ω.

This stores a concrete representative toFun and existential weak-derivative data. It does not identify functions modulo almost-everywhere equality; use SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.WkpSpaceOn for the Lp-quotient normed-space packaging.

For 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞ and open Ω, this is the representative-level condition defining W^{k,p}(Ω) in Evans §5.2.2. The order-zero witness is then redundant, but retaining it makes local integrability explicit when this structure is used at other exponents and prevents nonintegrable functions from entering through the totalized Bochner integral. On a nonopen set the structure uses the generalized test-function relation documented by HasWeakDerivativeOn, so the usual uniqueness theorem need not apply.

Localize a bounded extension of any finite Sobolev order to an arbitrary open neighborhood of closure Ω.

This gives condition (ii) of Evans §5.4, Theorem 1, "Eu has support within V", which Evans arranges in step 6 of the proof. We choose a smooth cutoff with support in V and equal to one on closure Ω, multiply the original extension by it, and retain both a.e. agreement on Ω and bounded linearity. The domain need only be measurable; the cutoff acts on the whole-space extension. This includes order zero and p = ∞.

Rellich compactness for H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω) under the operational Boundary.C1ExtensionAtlas hypothesis. The order-zero inclusion

H¹(Ω) → L²(Ω)

is compact when Ω carries the operational chart-and-cutoff data used by the extension theorem. Deriving this hypothesis from the standard assertion that Ω has C¹ boundary is a separate geometric step.

The proof factors the inclusion in four steps. Extension.C1.extensionCLM sends H¹(Ω) boundedly into H¹(ℝ^n) and agrees with the original base function almost everywhere on Ω. Multiplying by a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one on closure Ω and restricting to a ball B containing its support lands continuously in H¹₀(B). The bounded-domain Rellich theorem for H¹₀(B) makes zero extension followed by the base-coordinate map compact, and precomposition keeps it compact. Finally restriction L²(ℝ^n) → L²(Ω) is bounded, and since the cutoff is one on Ω the composite is the order-zero inclusion.

The direct method gives a unique weak solution of the odd-power Dirichlet equation

-Delta u + linear * u + nonlinear * u ^ (2 * k + 1) = f.

The analytic hypotheses require integrability of the potential energy, an L² representative N u of the polynomial nonlinearity for every u ∈ H¹₀, and Fréchet differentiability of the integral potential with derivative loadFunctional (N u). The theorem assumes these inputs; it does not derive them from a dimension or exponent restriction. By Sobolev embedding the representability hNrep holds for every k when n ≤ 2, and for 2 * k + 1 ≤ n / (n - 2) when n ≥ 3. Above that range, with nonlinear ≠ 0 and Ω open and nonempty, it fails and the theorem is vacuous.

if c then t else e is notation for ite c t e, "if-then-else", which decides to return t or e depending on whether c is true or false. The explicit argument c : Prop does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional [Decidable c] argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually determines how to evaluate c to true or false. Write if h : c then t else e instead for a "dependent if-then-else" dite, which allows t/e to use the fact that c is true/false.

Let n≥1, k>0, 1≤p, and kp=n. On a bounded domain with a supplied order-k extension operator, every W^{k,p} field belongs to L^q(Ω) for every finite q≥1.

When n=1, criticality forces k=p=1, and the bounded representative supplies every finite exponent. In higher dimensions, finite-measure monotonicity handles q≤n. For q>n, the choice s=nq/(n+q) gives 1≤s<n; the localized global W^{1,s} field then satisfies the first-order Sobolev theorem. SobolevSpace.Weighted.HasLocallyComparableExhaustion {n k : ℕ} (w : SobolevSpace.GraphSpace.DerivIndex n k → ℝ^n → ENNReal) : Prop

For every realizable weighted graph U and accuracy ε there are: a graph V within ε/3 of U in the w-norm, a bounded reference weight v with a dominated weight q, and a sequence of test functions converging to V in the v-norm whose w-distance to V is eventually at most the q-distance plus ε/3 (EventuallyDistLeWeightedDistAdd).

All witnesses, including the comparison constants B and C, are chosen per U and ε. Since q = v = 0 and V = U are admissible, the predicate is equivalent to approximation of every realizable weighted graph by eligible test functions in the w-norm, arranged in the shape of the localize-compare-mollify argument.

The hypotheses: the all-axial order-n row is C² and compactly supported in z, every order-n row is C² and compactly supported in r, Φmid is C¹ in r and in z, the weights are nonnegative and satisfy hcompare0, hcompare1_axial and hcompare1_radial, and the weighted squares and cross terms are integrable and the weighted rows measurable on the half plane. No row inequality is assumed.

The hypothesis hradial_axis requires every order-n row, including the pure-axial row ∂_z^n f, to vanish on the axis r = 0. This restricts the theorem to data all of whose order-n rows have zero axis trace: at n = 0 to functions vanishing on the axis, as odd profiles do, and for n ≥ 1 it excludes even profiles whose even-exponent rows need not vanish there.

Noncompact interpolation for all mixed derivatives of middle order n + 1.

The pure-axial row uses axial integration by parts; every positive-radial row uses radial integration by parts with its order-n predecessor. The successor identities identify both derivatives without commuting mixed partials. Local C² regularity is required only along these predecessor slices in r > 0, and the middle weight is differentiable there.

Weighted L² membership supplies the three square integrabilities and weighted measurabilities. The cross-term integrabilities and the two endpoint limits of each boundary product remain explicit. Neither compact support, a zero value trace on the axis, nor any row inequality is assumed.

Weight comparisons hold almost everywhere for the open-half-plane product measure. Zero extension supplies globally nonnegative weights to the Cauchy estimate without imposing conditions at the singular origin. The conclusion is one adjacent-order interpolation step.

One-dimensional Morrey inequality, the Hölder seminorm bound of Evans §5.6.2, Theorem 4, for n = 1 and with constant one.

For every 1 < p ≤ ∞, a continuously differentiable real-valued function satisfies

|u(y) - u(x)| ≤ ‖u'‖_{Lᵖ(ℝ)} |y - x|^(1 - 1/p).

The statement uses ℝ≥0∞ throughout, so it remains meaningful without a separate finiteness assumption on the global Lᵖ seminorm. When that seminorm is finite, the estimate gives the usual (1 - 1/p)-Hölder bound.

The Morrey Hölder exponent 1 - n / p. With Mathlib's convention ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0, this gives exponent 1 at p = ∞. The definition is total, but its analytic use is restricted by hypotheses such as n < p.

Multidimensional finite-exponent Morrey estimate for every C¹ function (Evans, PDE, §5.6.2, Theorem 4).

For 1 ≤ n < p < ∞, every C¹ real-valued function on ℝ^n satisfies

|u(y)-u(x)| ≤ C(n,p) ‖Du‖ₚ |y-x|^(1-n/p).

No geometric potential hypothesis remains. The proof combines enorm_sub_ballAverage_le_morreyPotential, Hölder's inequality, and the exact polar integral of the Morrey kernel. The explicit constant below includes the enlargement factors 2^n and 2^(1-n/p).

This is the global C¹(ℝ^n) estimate. Extending it to a Hölder representative of an arbitrary W^{1,p} class on a bounded C¹ domain is outside this theorem's scope.

The factor 2^n comes from the geometric inclusion B(c,R) ⊆ B(x,2R) when x ∈ B̄(c,R).

Multidimensional finite-exponent Morrey estimate (Evans, PDE, §5.6.2, Theorem 4).

Let 1 ≤ n < p < ∞ and let q be conjugate to p. If the same-ball point-to-average estimate and the kernel estimate hold with constants A and K, then every pair of points satisfies

|u(y)-u(x)| ≤ 2 A K ‖Du‖_{Lᵖ(ℝ^n)} |y-x|^(1-n/p).

The proof compares both points to the average on the same n-dimensional ball and applies Hölder's inequality to the Riesz kernels. The unconditional enlarged-ball theorem below has no geometric assumptions and an explicit dimension-dependent factor in its constant.
SobolevSpace.HasBallAveragePotentialBound u A

The same-ball point-to-average potential estimate.

For a point x in the closed ball B̄(c,R), the oscillation from the ball average is controlled by the Riesz potential of |Du| over B(c,R). This is the multidimensional segment-averaging theorem in the proof of Evans §5.6.2, Theorem 4.

enorm_sub_ballAverage_le_morreyPotential proves the enlarged-ball form needed for Morrey's inequality. The predicate records the same-ball estimate used by the conditional theorems; the main theorem does not assume it, and the predicate alone does not encode Hölder continuity.

If p and q are Hölder conjugates and p > n, polar integration gives this property with a constant depending only on n and p. The theorem hasMorreyKernelBound_of_holderConjugate below proves it from the exact centered-ball integral.
